### sacrifice paddock

 
<i>noun</i>.

>  The farming technique known as the `sacrifice' paddock, in which one paddock on a farm is heavily stocked during the winter to save pastures elsewhere on the farm for use by cattle after calving was criticised by the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals in the Palmerston North Magistrates' Court today. ... in Dalefield's case it had been the stock rather than the paddock which had been `sacrificed' <i>(Aug 14, 1958,Christchurch Star-Sun,13</i>)

>  <i>sacrifice paddock n. N.Z.</i> a grassed field which is allowed to be grazed completely, so that it can be cultivated and resown later. <i>(1982,Collins Concise English Dictionary,1015</i>) [NOTES: [nf. 1986 NZPOD; 1985 Collins NZ Compact Dict. 428]]

>  His practice of putting his herd in a "sacrifice" paddock is common among dairy farmers. Rather than damage all his farm moving his herd around in the mud, he opts to sacrifice poorly performing paddocks and later cultivate and resow them with a crop followed by new grass when the weather improves. <i>(Sep 9, 2004,Dominion Post,C7</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a fenced area on which a farmer will bring in silage, hay or other feed to stock in very wet weather , causing the sward to be pugged and trampled.

>  We fed 118 cows for a full month on this crop, supplemented by a 'sacrifice' paddock adjoining.. In wet weather we left the cows in the sacrifice paddock and fed hay out to them. <i>(Jun 10, 1958,NZ Dairy Exporter,29</i>)

>  <b>MCMEEKAN</b> The 'sacrifice paddock' system of wintering would be employed for the feeding-out of hay and silage during winter. <i>(1960,Grass to Milk,187</i>)

>  I used to think sacrifice paddocks were bound to be very fertile the next year and the heavier the stocking, the richer they'd be. <i>(Sep 10, 1970,NZ Farmer,61</i>)

>  Fortunately, the herd had to walk some distance from a 'sacrifice' paddock to the barn through a shingle bottomed stream, which is a first-class indicator of founder, or overheating of the feet. <i>(Sep 1973,NZ Journal of Agriculture,61</i>)

>  Sacrifice paddocks with feeding racks on platforms on the race-side border may be worth considering. <i>(Sep 27, 1973,NZ Farmer,7</i>)

>  I intend to throw away the backing wire, revert to the old 1950s practice of a 'sacrifice paddock' on the bad grub areas and really trample hell out of them. <i>(Jul 1983,NZ Journal of Agriculture,69</i>)

>  MAF is encouraging farmers to watch their image after complaints from townies and tourists over cattle being held in muddy sacrifice paddocks. <i>(Aug 1, 1996,NZ Farmer,4</i>)

### SADD

Sadd operates in more than 80% of Kiwi high schools and is run mostly by students. It aims to raise awareness about the dangers of drinking and driving. <i>(Nov 30, 2003,Sunday Star Times,A15</i>)

### saddletweed

 
<i>adjective</i>. [Rural] [of trousers] made of strong woollen twill fabric [teamed with tartan shirt and hobnailed boots as a high-country worker's 'uniform'].

>  <b>NEWTON</b> Even their working attire - the best of sports coats and saddle tweed trousers, which were in complete contrast to what I had been accustomed - set them apart. <i>(1947,Wayleggo,34</i>)

>  <b>DAVIS</b> In spite of the cold, the drizzle, and the clammy wetness of the grass which was starting to penetrate my thick saddle-tweed trousers... <i>(1962,Mutton on the Menu,115</i>)

>  <b>STAPLES</b> Old saddletweed trousers, tartan shirts and hob-nailed boots were their uniform till the weekend. <i>(1964,Cooks and Shepherds Come Away,95</i>)

>  <b>NEWTON</b> Drummond Fernie almost invariably dressed in a saddle tweed suit ... <i>(1969,Big Country of the North Island,151</i>)

>  <b>OGONOWSKA-COATES</b> .. some of the older shearers prefer saddle-tweed pants and a pair of braces. <i>(1987,Boards, Blades & Barebellies,41</i>)

>  <b>SINCLAIR & TROTTER</b> I was lucky I was well shod, O'Brien mustering boots on, my saddletweed trousers tied down, so I was dry as could be. <i>(1994,From Caithness to Southland,17</i>)

### saeeda

 
<i>exclamation</i>.

>  Sa-eeda Ahmed, Akers, arrak,/ Bints, Bomonti. backsheech, barrak;/ Centipedes and Cleopatra,/ Dust and desert, djinns and Fatima;/ `Eggs-cook, ana miskeen,'/ Fever, flies, and felaheen;/ Gehenam, Galabeyah, gods,/ Harems, hooshters, heat and hods;/ `Igri wallah, imshi Y'allah.'/ Jackos, jackals, `gala gala';/ Khamseen, kan kan, tala hena,/ Lice and locusts, love and Lena;/ Mirage, Mahomet, mosquistoe,/ Niggers, T.A.B. and C2;/ Olives oranges, askarie./ Peanuts, pyramids, and gharry;/ `Queens' and `Quacks' and `k'weis kateer,'/ Ruins, rum, and Gyppo beer;/ Scorpion, sand, sun, sin, and Scarab,/ Tibbin, taube, and tricky Arab;/ Whizz-bangs, wadis, `yin-al-deenak,'/ Yids, and yesterday, yeh meenak;/ Kestrels, kingfishers, and kites,/ Torrid days and sleepless nights;/ Mosques and minarets--maleesh;/ `O'ariglak,' `feluce--mafeesh'--/ Bookra, badein, ack-ack-emma,/ The soldier's farewell--ma-es salemma; <i>(Jul 10, 1919,Quick March,33</i>)

### safen

 
<i>verb</i>. to make safe

>  David Gregorie of Waikanae quotes a letter in his local paper from Niki Trotter, of Raumati Beach: "I find it hard to see why anyone would be against safening a very dangerous piece of road with an extremely bad accident history." Now that's a truly marvellous word. "Safen". to "make safe", follows all the best precedents, using that Germanic -en ending to make a verb out of an adjective. It mimics fasten, worsen, harden, sweeten, sharpen, shorten, stiffen etc. <i>(Apr 28, 2004,Dominion Post,B5</i>)

>  Therefore, the pressure is truly on Transit NZ to safety-proof, as far as it can, the highway people travelling to and from the capital from the west are forced to use. <i>(Oct 7, 2004,Dominion Post,B4</i>)

>  <b>TURNER</b>  <i>(1966,English Language in Aust. & NZ, The,150</i>)

Thursday was Sale Day, when the farmers came in to buy and sell sheep or calves, heifers and pigs, and the farmer's wife to trade her butter and eggs at the grocer's for stores, and to buy towels and sheets and shoes. Market day, they would call it in England, but there was no market in these small New Zealand towns. There were no stalls in the street or square, where the farmer and his wife sold poultry and apples, eggs and butter, fruit and cream. The cows and sheep and horses and other farm stock were gathered into pens at the saleyard, and sold by auction. <i>(1949,Rusty Road,10</i>)

>  <b>BIDWILL</b> Other shell-fish are also abundant, particularly Cockles - of these I have seen more than a man could carry collected by one woman during the space of a tide; Scallops are also tolerably abundant, and are most delicious eating. There are no Lobsters nor Crabs, but a great abundance of fish of all kinds; one, the Salmon of the English, or Carwai (Carwhy), is a most excellent fish, the best I have tasted in the Southern Hemisphere; ... <i>(1841,Rambles in NZ,115,1952</i>)

>  <b>POLACK</b> Among the piscivorous tribes, are those well known in Europe under the appellations of snapper, tench, haddocks, pollock, salmon, gurnets, john dory, hakes, bream, sword-fish, elephant-fish, diodons, pipe-fish, cod, parrot-fish, flounders, skate, cat and dog-fish, sting-rays, eels. - Among the larger tribes that sport in shoals in the vicinity of the shore, are, sperm-whales, called <i>para[as-acute]<i> paraua</i> [a3-acute] (physeter macrocephalus); black whale, <i> mungu nui</i>  (black physeter); right whale, <i>tohora</i>  (balaena mysticetus); finback, (balaena physalis); sun-fish (diodon mola); large-lipped whale (balaena mysticetus); large-lipped whale (balaena musculus); hump-back (balaena gibbosa); shark, <i> mango</i>  (squalus); hammer-head (zygaena); pilots, (scomber); flying-fish (exocaetus volitans); and an infinity of others, besides a great variety of testaceous and crustaceous fishes that almost cover the rocks under water, such as clams, muscles, oysters, crays, cuttles, limpets, wilks, gigantic muscles, a foot in length, cockles, sea-ears, sea-eggs, star-fish, mutton-fish, &c.; from the latter the pearl is procured which they insert in the eyes of their carved images and boxes. <i>(1840,Manners & Customs of the NZers,1/202 fn</i>)

>  <b>MORRIS</b> <i> Salmon, n</i> . The English Salmon is being acclimatised with difficulty in Tasmania and New Zealand; the <i>Trout</i>  more successfully. The fish is often called also <i> Salmon-Trout.</i>  The young is called <i> Samson-fish</i>  (q.v.). <i>(1898,Austral English,400</i>)

### salube

 
<i>verb</i>.

[NOTES: ca1938 (R. Mason)]

>  <b>MACLEAN</b> [John Pascoe] appreciated fitness, though not speed, and above all he appreciated relaxation, especially sunbathing. To promote this concept he coined the term 'to salube', which soon became synonymous with his name and has become part of Tararua folklore. <i>(1994,Tararua : the Story of a Mountain Range,174</i>)



 
<i>adjective</i>.

>  To offset these rather gloomy expressions there are those that derive from <i> salubrious.</i>  They are J.D. Pascoe terms and were brought by him from Canterbury to Wellington. They obviously arose from the habit of describing sunny, pleasant weather or places as `salubrious'. First is the <i> salubrium</i> , a rest or sunbake in salubrious conditions. This first appeared in <i> The Tramper</i>  in 1937. About 1939 people were <i> salubriating</i> , or taking a <i> salube</i>  in the sun. The previous year Te Matawai was described as a `salube hut'. By 1943 trampers were sunbathing and <i> salubing</i> . So far as Tararuas are concerned,<i> salube</i>  as a noun and a verb is the word that has survived. <i>(Sep 1958,Tararua,28</i>) [NOTES: 1958 Sep Ruth Mason `Track and Trail' in Tararua 28]



 
<i>noun</i>. a period of relaxation (in the sun)

[NOTES: (Ruth Mason: from <i> salubrious</i>)]

>  <b>MASON</b> SALUBE n and v: a tramping term c1938: Wellington only I think. Not as common as it once was. <i>(Jun 7, 1952,Personal Communication</i>) [NOTES: a1938 p.c. R. Mason June 7 1952 (Wellington)]

>  To offset these rather gloomy expressions there are those that derive from <i> salubrious.</i>  They are J.D. Pascoe terms and were brought by him from Canterbury to Wellington. They obviously arose from the habit of describing sunny, pleasant weather or places as `salubrious'. First is the <i> salubrium</i> , a rest or sunbake in salubrious conditions. This first appeared in <i> The Tramper</i>  in 1937. About 1939 people were <i> salubriating</i> , or taking a <i> salube</i>  in the sun. The previous year Te Matawai was described as a `salube hut'. By 1943 trampers were sunbathing and <i> salubing</i> . So far as Tararuas are concerned,<i> salube</i>  as a noun and a verb is the word that has survived. <i>(Sep 1958,Tararua,28</i>) [NOTES: 1958 Sep Ruth Mason `Track and Trail' in Tararua 28]

>  <b>TURNER</b> <i> Salubrious <i>... became a common word for good weather and developed many derivatives, e.g.<i> salubing</i> `sunbathing', <i>salubriating</i> `taking a <i>salube'</i>, and <i>salubrium</i> `rest in the sun'. <i>(1966,English Language in Aust. & NZ, The,161</i>)

### Samoan cricket

 
<i>noun</i>.

See: kilikiti

[NOTES: see also Pacific cricket]

>  I presume you do not know that in a Samoan cricket match there will be fifty or sixty players aside [sic], and one match will probably last several days. <i>(Mar 31, 1888,Te Aroha News,4</i>)

>  When it is added that the bowling is fast and throwing, at which Samoens [sic] are most expert, is allowed, that the bat is shaped like a long and heavy broomstick, tapering from four inches to two, and the ball is made of hard and heavy wood bound with cocoanut fibre, it will be seen that Samoan cricket presents many novel features. <i>(Dec 27, 1901,Poverty Bay Herald,1</i>)

>  [Arthur Tyndall] was impressed by the luxuriant plant growth in Samoa and by the great abundance of of amusements, Samoan cricket, singing, dancing and the King's Birthday sports at Apia. <i>(Apr 1987,NZ Journal of History,148</i>) [NOTES: (Boyd)]

>  KILIKITI: Samoan cricket bears about as much resemblance to the ... territory of Lords as the sound of the word does to English. ... For one thing the bat - fashioned in triangular shape from the springy fau tree, decorated in gaudy splashes of colour and bound with coconut fibre - has nothing to do with the sissy wider blade of the willow. It's an out-and-out war club of such bold length ... The ball, spun by hand from liquid rubber tapped from a living tree and compressed to rock-hard consistency, bounds down the pitch with a dangerously unpredictable velocity. ... [T]eams are of indefinite size - 15 a side is considered a minimum for serious competitions... When the batting team reaches 35 runs, to keep the action alive, the teams swop over. <i>(May 1987,Metro,110</i>)

### sandfly

 
<i>noun</i>. Austrosimulium spp. (fam. Simuliidae), a common small black native fly

See: also namu

>  The sandflies are not very terrible. <i>(Jan 9, 1896,Otago Witness,51</i>)

>  The intelligent and influential citizen.. should he at any time prefer the company of sandflies to the polite courtesies of the city rate-collector, would here (sc. Fiordland) find a quiet and undisturbed retreat. <i>(Feb 22, 1879,Auckland Weekly News,10</i>)

>  Oh! what awful plagues the mosquitoes and sandflies are. <i>(Mar 1938,NZ Railways Magazine,41</i>) [NOTES: Quote from Scott, 1860]

>  Our camp was besieged with sand-flies. <i>(Mar 6, 1890,Otago Witness,35</i>)

>  <b>HOCHSTETTER</b> The sandflies, on the other hand, the Ngamu of the natives, small midges (Simulium), are most frequent on the sea coast. <i>(1867,New Zealand (Hochstetter),287</i>)

>  With nothing but a sodden fly between you and the crescendous Fiordland rainclouds, the sandflies - "black hordes of little devils" - are free to feast upon you in waves. <i>(Feb 12, 2005,Dominion Post,E14</i>)

>  Our hunger was nothing compared to that of the infamous Fiordland sandflies. <i>(Nov 23, 2003,Sunday Star Times,C13</i>)

>  The sandflies were numerous and ravenous. <i>(Sep 6, 1890,NZ Observer,6</i>)

>  Te Aroha is noted for.. the lavish attention bestowed on visitors by its sandflies. <i>(Jan 27, 1912,NZ Free Lance,6</i>)

>  They both grew weaker bye and bye, / The Old Man and the Big Sandfly. <i>(1969,AUTC Song Book (3rd ed.),Song No. 61</i>)

>  <b>BREMER</b> He brought out a tin of engine oil and we covered our hands and wrists with oil and let the sandflies drown in it. <i>(1983,Port Craig,28</i>)

>  <b>ORBELL</b> The backs of the hands are the places where the sandflies seem to prefer most and if you are skinning a big stag in sandfly country, you will realise how deadly they can be. <i>(1952,Comfort & Commonsense in the Bush,32</i>)

>  The Student's Association needed [Union Hall] to house people working on the summer newspaper "Sandfly". <i>(Mar 15, 1982,Salient,1</i>)

>  This was the Avon, one of a little fleet of sandfly craft built and armed for service on the Waikato and Waipa rivers. <i>(Dec 28, 1912,NZ Free Lance,5</i>)

>  There's an especially great take with the roast fillet of sandfly recipe! <i>(Apr 13, 2000,Evening Post,Living Style : 2</i>)

>  Three days earlier, on a drawn-out West Coast mid-summer evening, when sandflies the size of apple pips suck the blood from my ankles, two Westport members of Native Forest Action also took me to Station Creek. <i>(Apr 2000,North & South,84</i>)

>  Peter Urlich, God bless him, is an incurable show-off. He admits it in a recent <i>Metro</i> magazine piece) along with arrogance, philandering, being a poor listener with the attention span of a sandfly. <i>(Jul 23, 2000,Sunday Star Times,F4</i>)

>  The hon. member compared them to irritating sandflies - "namu" was the word he used - and the Chief Commissioner to a big "namu." <i>(Sep 15, 1860,Hawke's Bay Herald,1</i>)

>  We stole a march a march on the sandflies at "Cascade," where we had an iron chimney to our tent. <i>(Mar 12, 1896,Otago Witness,46</i>)

>  But many a beach and picturesque bush camp is infested by mosquitoes, sandflies, or other stinging insects. <i>(Jan 16, 1930,NZ Truth,17</i>)

>  <b>CRANK</b> There are not many ... insects ... [187] only a few dragon-flies, butterflies, grasshoppers, spiders, and black-ants, vast numbers of scorpion-flies, and a sand-fly ... <i>(1830,New Zealanders, The,186</i>)

>  <b>FORSTER</b> We had been plagued all the time of our stay [at Dusky Bay] by a very minute black <i>Tipula alis incumbentibus,</i> which the people called a <i>Sandfly</i>: its Sting is very painfull & causes ... a most intolerable itching .. <i>(Apr 3, 1773,Resolution Journal of J.R. Forster, The,2/246</i>)

>  <b>FORSTER</b> ... a sort of little crane-flies (<i>tipula alis incumbentibus</i>), which had plagued us ever since our entrance into Dusky Bay, became remarkably troublesome during the bad weather. They were numerous in the [136] skirts of the woods, not half so large as gnats or musketoes, and our sailors called them sand-flies. <i>(1777,Voyage Round the World,1/135</i>)

>  <b>BELL</b> - nor in short did we see any living thing on shore except the Birds - a small Sand fly - but this annoy'd us more than perhaps fifty animals wou'd - <i>(1791,Journal of Voyage in HMS 'Chatham',51</i>)

>  <b>YATE</b> ... a small sand-fly, not larger than a flea, but very noxious - its bite is sharp, and leaves an unpleasant itching for many hours ... <i>(1835,New Zealand (various authors/titles),72</i>)

>  <b>HALL-JONES</b> ... the sand-flies were rife ... <i>(1971,Mutton Birds & Other Birds,57</i>) [NOTES: (Griffiths Collection) 1850s in 1971 Hall-Jones Mr Surveyor Thomson 57]

>  <b>MACKIE</b> Mosquitos and sand flies ( a small black fly) I find very troublesome, they inflame my hands very much. <i>(Feb 14, 1853,Traveller under Concern,79,1973</i>)

>  <b>TINNE</b> Fleas, Maori bugs, sand-flies and mosquitoes were bad enough .. <i>(1873,Wonderland of the Antipodes,52</i>)

>  <b>PRESHAW</b> sandflies <i>(1888,Banking Under Difficulties</i>) [NOTES: (Griffiths Collection) 1888 Preshaw 104 quoting 1864]

>  <b>DIEFFENBACH</b> <i>Simulium </i>? Namu, or sand-fly. <i>Polack,</i> New Zeal., p.319. ... To some insect, of a genus allied to Simulium, is to be referred the New Zealand sand-fly alluded to in the following passage:- `A sort of little crane-flies (<i>tipula alis incumbentibus</i>) became remarkably troublesome during the bad weather. They were numerous in the skirts of the woods, not half so large as gnats or musketoes, and our sailors called them sand-flies. Their sting was extremely painful. . . . All, however, were not equally affected.' Forster, Voyage, ., pp. 135, 136. `The most mischievous animals (at Dusky Bay) are the small black sand-flies, which are very numerous, and so troublesome, that they exceed everything of the kind I ever met with: wherever they bite they cause a swelling ...' Cook, Voyage in Resolution and Adventure, i., p.99. <i>(1849,Travels in NZ,2/290</i>) [NOTES: 1843 Dieffenbach Travels in NZ 2/290 [quoting Forster]]

>  The little gunboat <i>Sandfly</i> had them [sc. Maoris] at her mercy. <i>(Oct 1937,NZ Railways Magazine,38</i>)

### sandpaper suit

 
<i>noun</i>. a school cadet uniform

>  We had to put up on Anzac Day with our sandpaper suits. <i>(May 4, 2001,Radio NZ / National Radio</i>)

>  Whatever happened to those `sandpaper suits?' - the khaki shorts and battledress tunics worn by thousands of boys during the heyday of the school cadets. He understood the uniforms went out of use some time in the 1960s. <i>(Jul 29, 1983,Evening Post</i>)

### sandshoe

### sandy back

 
<i>noun</i>. a sheep with sand, grit, or dirt in the back wool

>  <b>BOWEN</b>  <i>(1956,Wool Away!,157</i>)

>  <b>TURNER</b> There are names for types of sheep, the <i>cot</i> with matted wool; <i>the cobbler</i>, a difficult one; the <i>flyer</i>, a fast one; the <i>kicker</i>; the <i>sandyback</i> and the gasper, which gasps apparently because grass comes into its throat. <i>(1966,English Language in Aust. & NZ, The,147</i>)

>  <b>McLEOD</b> <i>Sandy-backs</i>: Sheep which have rubbed sand and stones into the wool by scratching under banks. <i>(1972,Mountain World,310</i>)

>  <i>Sandyback</i>: Sheep with sand, grit, or dirt in the back wool SANDY BACK. A sheep with sand, grit of dirt in the back wool. <i>(1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,58</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] 1. a sheep with fine sand and dirt in its wool [after rubbing in dirt or small stones.] 2. the fleece from such a sheep.

See: shivey back; seedy back

>  <b>BOWEN</b> Sandy Back. A sheep with sand, grit or dirt in the back wool. <i>(1955,Wool Away!,157</i>)

>  <b>MASTERS</b> On strolling along and glancing casually into Syke's catching pens, I noticed that he had eight tough looking, old sandy-backs in it. <i>(1960,Back-Country Tales,257</i>)

>  <b>LOUGHNAN</b> sandy back: a sheep that has been relieving irritation by rubbing against a bank and has thus rubbed sand and small pebbles into its wool. <i>(1981,Loughnan Glossary,69</i>)

>  <b>MAF</b> Sandy back: sheep with sand, grit, or dirt in the back wool. 2. <i>(1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,58</i>)

>  <b>DOMINY</b> .. bins and bales for belly wool, top knots, skirting wool, sandy and seedy backs if they are present ... [sandy back] <i>(2001,Calling the Station Home,190</i>)

### sandy backed

 
<i>adjective</i>. [Rural] [of sheep] with fine stones and sand rubbed into wool on their backs.

See: shingle-backed

[NOTES: also sandy-backed]

>  While the squatters could get men to travel out back from 500 to 1000 miles and put up with mutton, damper, black sugar, and blacker tea for 15s to 17s 6d a week, and pig-up in dens unfit for pigs; and so long as men could be got to shear sandy-backed and burr-infected sheep for 15s a hundred, and travel hundreds of miles to and from the sheds, the squatters never sought to improve the conditions or increase the rate of pay, but the expansion of the pastoral industry kept on apace, and the present set-back is but the result of years of thoughtlessness and bad management. <i>(Oct 22, 1902,Otago Witness,13</i>)

>  <b>NEWTON</b> He'd been only a few seconds over three minutes, which was pretty good time for a sandy-backed Merino wether. <i>(1949,High Country Days,50</i>)

>  <b>STRONACH</b> .. the wethers were sandy-backed and hard shearing - things sounded busy back at the station. <i>(1953,Musterer on Molesworth,29</i>)

>  <b>MASTERS</b> Frank Nurse and the musterers .. kept the tough old sandy-backed wethers well out of sight. [sandy backed] <i>(1960,Back-Country Tales,256</i>)

### Save Manapouri

 
<i>noun</i>. [Environment] a term used from 1959 for a nationwide protest against the raising of Lake Manapouri to high levels for hydroelectricity generation.

[NOTES: also Save Manapouri campaign]

>  MANAPOURI stickers seem to come in a number of different forms. There is the common "Save Manapouri," a simple plea from the heart. "Help Save Manapouri," a call not to be just sympathetic but do something about it. Then there is "I Want to Save Manapouri," a pitiful cry by someone who feels impotent to do anything. But my favourite is the cynic's sticker indicating that he is tired of the whole business: "Drain Manapouri." <i>(Mar 2, 1970,Evening Post,32</i>)

>  The 1970 Save Manapouri petition was the third to be drawn up with the object of preserving the lake and was the largest petititon ever to be presented to Parliament. <i>(Aug 1970,Forest & Bird,8</i>)

>  Within the past 12 months we have received powerful support from "Save Manapouri" committees, which have been organised throughout the country. <i>(May 1970,Forest & Bird,10</i>)

>  <b>Neville PEAT</b> Save Manapouri is a cry deeply embedded in the collective consciousness of New Zealanders and is still capable of being dusted off. <i>(1994,Manapouri Saved,10</i>)

>  PLEA MADE FOR PRESERVATION. 'Swift Action Needed to Save Manapouri' [hdg]. <i>(Oct 21, 1959,Evening Post,22</i>)

>  Exploratory Talks Here on How to Save Manapouri   [hdg] Substantial interest had been shown in the activities of the Save Manapouri Committee ... <i>(Jan 20, 1970,Evening Post,15</i>)

>  <b>Roger WILSON</b> The turning point of the opposition to the raising of the lake came when a crowded and lively public meeting was held in Invercargill  on 30 October [1969]. As a result of that meeting, the first "Save Manapouri" committee was set up. Similar groups were quickly established in other centres around the country. <i>(1982,From Manapouri to Aramoana,15</i>)

>  The movement to "Save Manapouri" is a case book example of how trends are adopted in a democratic society. <i>(Apr 1970,Comment,4</i>)

### Save Manapouri campaign

 
<i>noun</i>. [Environment] an extensive nationwide campaign to prevent high level raising of Lake Manapouri for hydroelectricity generation.

>  The Save Manapouri campaign has been lauded as "the birth of the modern conservation movement" in New Zealand. The Save Manapouri campaign began in the late 1950s with the proposal to build a power station to supply power to an aluminium smelter in the far south of New Zealand and gained momentum in the 1960s when it was proposed that the level of Lake Manapouri would be raised 8.2 metres to harness its hydro-electric potential for the project. <i>(May 7, 2008,Internet - see Notes,1</i>) [NOTES: www.forestandbird.org.nz/what-we-do/publications/forest-bird-magazine/article]

>  Among other things he was - with his wife - a driver of the Save Manapouri campaign, which succeeded in preventing the Crown from raising the level of the lake by some eight metres to generate electricity for the Bluff smelter. <i>(Feb 26, 2009,Dominion Post,B3</i>) [NOTES: from obituary of Dr Ian Prior - refer dawn raid and overstayer]

>  <b>Neville PEAT</b> The Save Manapouri Campaign lifted the lid. New Zealand had seen nothing of its kind before. It was a phenomenon in public awareness, concern and agitation. <i>(1994,Manapouri Saved,3</i>)

>  In an effort to discern basic attitudes to the issue of the southern lakes' exploitation for power, members of Parliament are to be sent questionnaires by the Save Manapouri Campaign. <i>(Aug 21, 1972,Evening Post,3</i>)

>  And he [Mr R J McLean] said he thought that out of the Save Manapouri Campaign would evolve a permanent organisation to fight for the people of New Zealand when their natural environment was threatened by foreign or local industrialists, local bodies, or by their own Government. <i>(Feb 21, 1970,Evening Post,7</i>)

>  <b>Roger WILSON</b> The Save Manapouri Campaign was well funded and had a professional approach to publicity. <i>(1982,From Manapouri to Aramoana,11</i>)

<i>noun</i>. a new boy

<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a highly-infectious disease of sheep, caused by a mite Dematodecles ovis [rife among NZ flocks between 1845 and 1892.]

>  <b>ACLAND</b> Glenmark was one of the last runs in Canterbury to be clean of scab. <i>(1946,Early Canterbury Runs,274</i>)

>  SCAB. - Let emigrants in the cabin who are likely to possess sheep, carry out with them the little volume of Cunningham, "Hints to Emigrants" - the best receipts are there for curing the scab. <i>(Feb 3, 1844,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,3</i>)

>  The scab boiler sheds produced a hell-brew based on tobacco leaves, into which the sheep were slung to rid them of the dreaded mange mite. <i>(Mar 21, 1992,Dominion,4</i>)

>  <b>McRAE</b> Edgar Jones to destroy all his sheep, numbering 5,000, some or all said to be infected with scab. <i>(1963,By the Braes of Balquether,57</i>)

>  <b>McCASKILL</b> He [sc. Fowler] has scab at Tophouse and has neither the capital nor the skill to keep country like the Rainbow clean.<i>IBid.</i> 70 Scab is caused by a mite (not an insect, but a relation of spiders). The eggs are laid on the skin at the base of the wool fibres. The young mites puncture the epidermis and suck lymph. Small pustules develop from which a liquid exudes, coagulating to form a hard, pale-yellow crust, the scab. ... Infected sheep rub against rocks, posts ... and will bite at the skin, causing serious damage to the wool. ...Some flocks were affected as early as 1848, the Nelson area having serious trouble for many years after that. <i>(1969,Molesworth,56</i>) [NOTES: Quote from ACTON-ADAMS 1885]

<i>noun</i>. any of the cushion plants, most of which are native to New Zealand. <i>Raoulia lutescens</i>

>  A [caption] Windward slope, scabweed and <i>Poa maniototo</i>. <i>(1939,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,20/230</i>)

>  A [caption] Windward slope, scabweed and <i>Poa maniototo</i>. <i>(1939,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,20/230</i>)

### scale

 
<i>verb</i>. to adjust a set of examination marks up or down

>  Right now you get a set of marks, which is meaningless because it is scaled. <i>(Feb 17, 2001,Listener (New Zealand Listener),28</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. (esp. in phr. do a scale) a hurried departure (often to avoid reponsibilities or debts)

See: scaler

>  <i>The Scaler</i>: He hates to pay his Union fees / And holds out to the last / .... He's not the man to say `goodbye' / Before he hits the trail / He waits until his dues are due / The bloke who does a scale. <i>(1926,Transport Workers' Song Book,5</i>)

>  <b>BAKER</b>  <i>(1941,NZ Slang,52, 62</i>) [NOTES: [see SCALED, SCALER]]



 
<i>noun</i>. a flake of gold

See: cf. scaly gold

>  ... a hole was dug ..., and a quantity of the soil washed, but without any visible satisfactory result ... [A] favourable indication was noticed at a bar in the creek, and a quantity of the gravel and earth removed, a panful was taken from about two feet below the surface and washed, it produced a number of scales of gold. <i>(Nov 9, 1852,NZ Government Gazette,V/26/165</i>) [NOTES: 1852 Nov 9 NZGG (Report of Sub-Committee on Recent Gold Discovery in the Coromandel District) V/26/165]

>  <b>REED</b> At the bank I was interested seeing the gold being weighed ... The gold is what is called `scale', in little flat pieces, varying in size from a pin's head to a threepenny bit. <i>(1973,Annals of Early Dunedin,15</i>) [NOTES: c1861 Mrs J.W.Stack in 1973 Reed Annals of Early Dunedin 15]

>  <b>HAAST</b> ... I instructed my men to dig for gold; we found, to use a technical expression, `the colour everywhere'. They were generally thin, small scales, often only slightly rolled, and could not, therefore have been brought any distance. <i>(1879,Geology of the Provinces of Canterbury & Westland,84</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. to rush, go fast

[NOTES: ca1950 Look at it scaling along at 60 (used also with other preps. eg scale off =rush away)]

>  <b>BAKER</b> When we are taken down financially we are <i>scaled</i> [as in Australia] <i>(1941,NZ Slang,62</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. to swindle, cheat; steal

>  <b>PARTRIDGE</b> To steal; to rob (someone): Australian: since ca. 1925. Baker, 1942. See Scaler, 1, and cf. :- <i>(1949,Dictionary of the Underworld,596</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. to over-ride (deliberately) a section on a tram or bus; to cheat on the payment of one's fare

[NOTES: ca1951 Wellington F.M. O'Brien]

>  <i>scale, scale a ride v.t. </i>and i. ride on a tram, bus or other vehicle without paying whence, <i>scaler</i>. <i>(1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),17</i>)

The term "scarfies" was derived from the fact that because of the weather, the students usually wore scarves, often in the Otago colours of blue and gold. <i>noun</i>. a marble game

>  <b>SUTTON-SMITH</b> It is important to distinguish these `Action-Terms' of marbles from the innumerable merely descriptive marble terms which have no effect on the course of the action - terms such as Ringer, In, Smug, Dead Stick, Skun, Skinned, Sported off, Scat, Cannons, Dubs, Kills, Funs, Keeps, Pink. <i>(1953,Unorganized Games,2/770</i>)

>  <b>SUTTON-SMITH</b> Some of the typical terms used in marbles referred to the act of shooting and the movement of the marbles. Those related to ways of shooting marbles were cribbing, firsts, fudging, funks, funnicks, funnigans, flunks, forces, knee-high, knuckle-down-stiff, knuckles, and lasts. Terms connected with the movement of the marbles were: cannons, clears, dead-stick, double-hits, fires, funs, gees, haystacks, in smug, keeps, kills, kisses, lay-ups, manyes, ones, pink, ringer, rolls, scat, screws, skinned, skun, spiders, sported-off, stays, stops, tracks, throughs. (marbles) <i>Ibid.</i> 176 [Waitara, Taranaki, 1899: reference, game of Little Ring] Many heated arguments arose as to who said `everythings' or `nothings' first. If a player's `taw' touched a marble and lay alongside it, the others would shout `knuckle down' just before his turn. ... `Knuckle down' meant that the player had to hold his taw close to the marble attacked and fire it in that very inconvenient position. ... When a boy lost all his marbles at play he was `scat' [?related to skint ?HWO] . ... A `ringer' was a taw which, when fired at the commencement of the game, lodged in the track of the ring itself; that, and knocking a marble out when he `fired' were the perfect shots. ... To fire a shot while holding the hand nearer to the ring than where the taw had lain, was to `funk', an unforgiveable crime. <i>(1972,Folkgames of Children,175</i>)

>  <b>PARKER</b> There are eleven species of Native Ducks belonging to nine genera, all found elsewhere, except two--the little Flightless Duck of the Auckland Islands (genus <i>Nesonetta</i>) and the Blue Mountain Duck (<i>Hymenolamus</i>). Among the most interesting of the non-endemic forms, are the Paradise Duck or Sheldrake (<i>Casarca variegata</i>), the Brown Duck (<i>Anas chlorotis</i>), the Shoveller or Spoonbill duck (<i>Rhynchaspis variegata</i>), and the Scaup or Black Teal (<i>Fuligula Novae-Zealandiae</i>).' <i>(1889,Catalogue NZ Exhibition,117</i>)

### schnapper

 
<i>noun</i>. variant of snapper q.v.

>  <b>WILSON</b> SNAPPER ... The common name `snapper' was given to the fish by Captain Cook in 1770. He mistook it for a member of the true snapper family <i>Lutjanidae </i>, a group of fish with which he had become familar in American waters. Although he did mistake the fish Captain Cook spelt the name correctly, whereas many subsequent writers have used `schnapper' - an erroneous spelling of unknown origin. Perhaps some of the early snapper fishermen took bottles of schnapps along on their outings, hence going `schnapping'! <i>(1981,Fisherman's Bible,226</i>)

>  [species name] schnapper .. [scientific name] -- [other name(s)] See SNAPPER <i>Chrysophrys auratus </i> .. [other name(s)] schnapper, tamure. See also premium snapper [occas. BREAM] <i>(Jul 23, 1986,Codes for Species in NZ Waters</i>)

>  <b>PARROTT</b> The name `Snapper' is frequently spelled `Schnapper', but there appears no sound reason for this spelling; older authors especially, have used the spelling, but it is seldom seen in modern works on fishes. <i>Ibid.</i> 170 Snapper Chrysophrys auratus Schnapper <i>(1957,Sea Anglers' Fishes of NZ,99</i>)

>  schnapper A large common edible sea fish of Australia and New Zealand. <i>(1958,Whitcombe's Modern Junior Dictionary (8th edn),355</i>)

>  Wilkins went down town to.. beg the necessary meat for bait with which we were to catch the unsuspecting schnapper. <i>(Apr 26, 1890,NZ Observer,12</i>)

>  ...I thought I should economise and not buy schnapper, which is ridiculously expensive and which I still can't spell. <i>(Jun 29, 2002,Listener (New Zealand Listener),17</i>)

>  <b>DEVANNY</b> Sometimes as many as twenty schnapper would be caught. <i>(1928,Dawn Beloved,102</i>)

>  His sorrow at the struggles of the dying schnapper was pitiful to behold. <i>(Mar 5, 1904,NZ Observer,7</i>)

>  The barns were stored with glorious schnapper. <i>(Jun 28, 1913,NZ Observer,17</i>)

>  Poor Hansard, known as the "Dying Schnapper", was there. <i>(Oct 1, 1887,Auckland Weekly News,7</i>)

>  Instead, I got some freshly cooked pipi and raw schnapper. <i>(Oct 6, 2001,Listener (New Zealand Listener),93</i>)

>  Bellamy's menu has qualified as the most snobbish of all State papers. Whenever the well-known New Zealand fish called snapper is an item of Parliamentary diet it is invariable [sic] spelled `schnapper.' The gourmets of the Food and Wine Society could be forgiven for such literary heresy, but the old prosaic spelling should be good enough for the dining-room in Parliament House. Incidentally, the legend is that the fish was given the name `snapper' by Captain Cook when he was here on his voyage of exploration in 1770. As he and the members of his crew leaned over the side of their galleon two centuries ago and threw their fishing lines into the waters off the New Zealand coast the fish used to snap at the bait. Hence the name snapper. <i>(Mar 5, 1956,Dominion,8</i>)

>  My reference in last week's column to the snobbishness of Bellamy's in using the spelling `schnapper' when that fish was on its menu has brought `bites' galore - from fish merchants to schoolmasters. Most of them, it is fair to say, have taken up the cudgels on behalf of Bellamy's, but none of them has disproved my argument that the correct spelling is `snapper.' ... Some historians support my Captain Cook theory, though there are others who place the first use of the name `snapper' at a later date, certainly not earlier. They think the name may have been given the fish by Captain W. L. Edwardson, the commander of a New South Wales Government cutter called the Snapper which was in New Zealand waters in 1822 and 1823 investigating sealing prospects. He gave the name Port Snapper to an inlet on Ruapuke Island in Foveaux Strait. Whatever the origin of the word, the fish served at Bellamy's is indigenous to New Zealand and is spelt `snapper.' <i>(Mar 12, 1956,Dominion,8</i>)

>  The fishing off the island is very good, there being abundance of hapuku, kohikohi, maumau, schnapper, kahawai, tarakihi, in addition to plenty of shell-fish such as koura or cray-fish, crabs, paua,etc. <i>(1885,TrNZI,17/419</i>) [NOTES: (Goldsmith)]

>  <b>SHERRIN</b> SCHNAPPER (<i>Pagrus unicolor </i>). ... Dr. Hector says: `There are few fishes better known in the northern parts of the Colony than the schnapper. This name, by which it is known, is adopted from Australia, its Maori name, tamure, being seldom used by Europeans. It represents in these seas the braize of the European markets, ...' <i>(1886,Handbook Fishes of NZ,85</i>)

>  <b>SARA MATHEW</b> ... very fine fish they are [off Whangarei] - schnappers, gurnet and what is called salmon in these seas. <i>(Apr 20, 1840,Journal</i>) [NOTES: 1840 Apr 20 Sarah Mathew Journal in 1940 Founding of NZ 121]

>  <b>HAY</b> We have, indeed, a wealth of fish in all the tidal waters. Sharks, schnapper, rock-cod, mackerel, mullet, herring, sole, halibut, albacore, barracouta, king-fish, and others. <i>(1882,Brighter Britain,2/230</i>)

>  <b>MORRIS</b> <i>Schnapper </i> or <i> Snapper </i>... a fish abundant in all Australasian waters, <i>Pagrus unicolor </i>, Cuv. and Val. The latter spelling was the original form of the word (one that snaps). It was gradually changed by the fishermen, perhaps of Dutch origin, to <i>Schnapper </i>, the form now general. The name <i>Snapper </i> is older than the settlement of Australia, but it is not used for the same fish. `O.E.D.,' s.v. <i>Cavally </i>, quotes: ... In New Zealand, the <i>Tamure </i> (q.v.) is also called <i>Schnapper </i>, and the name <i>Red-Schnapper i </i>s given to <i>Anthias richardsoni </i>, Gunth., or <i> Scorpis hectori </i>, Hutton. <i>(1898,Austral English,404</i>)

### school shark

 
<i>noun</i>. lemon fish, flake, also called tope a shark of Australian and New Zealand waters, similar to the dogfish, but larger

>  <b>GRAHAM</b> TOPE OR SCHOOL SHARK <i>Notogaleus rhinophanes</i>  (Peron) The origin of the vernacular name Tope is not certain, but local fishermen who followed this occupation in Britain, said this name is a corruption of `top' in allusion to its well-known habit of following the lines to the top of the water and then snatching off Whiting or other hooked fish in full view of the helpless fisherman. Other New Zealand common names are Southern Tope and School Shark. <i>(1956,NZ Fishes: An Identification Guide,63</i>)

>  <b>WILSON</b> SCHOOLSHARK Not unlike a larger version of the Gummy shark (who grows to about four feet) the Schoolshark gets up to about eight feet and inhabits our [225] coastal waters ... The flesh, like that of the gummies, is quite edible and regularly marketed, usually at Lemonfish. The Schoolshark is usually dark-grey-green above and white below. Known also as Tope and Sand shark they are the only fish who close their eyes when they sleep. <i>(1981,Fisherman's Bible,224</i>)

>  The hoki are sent down first and are by far the major species caught in this area designated G in New Zealand's exclusive economic zone. But there are also ling and school shark, headed and gutted before they are boxed, squid and silver dory, fat blue nose and silver warehou, hake and sharp-toothed southern kingfish, ugly green monkfish and slimy flathead, electric skates and others with saw toothed snouts. <i>(Aug 22, 1984,Marlborough Express,6</i>)

### schooner

 
<i>noun</i>. an large beer glass or handle, holding about (?) twenty ounces. (aka Greymouth or West Coast schooner)

>  [The young men] were usually very thirsty and drank from long glasses, or "schooners." <i>(Feb 26, 1945,NZEF Times,IV/192 : 7</i>)

>  He doesn't say we never saw a schooner of beer, or that there are no barmaids in the country. <i>(Dec 15, 1906,New Zealand Free Lance,3</i>)

>  Everyone.. has heard of the renowned West Coast "schooners", enormous beer-glasses. <i>(Aug 27, 1947,NZ Observer,12</i>)

>  A practical joker, a prudent man withal, had gone to a cafe [sic] and ordered a "three-masted schooner" of beer, when a friend appears at the door and beckons him to go out for a minute. <i>(Nov 10, 1880,Taranaki Herald,4</i>) [NOTES: Cafe is spelt with a grave accent, as opposed to correct accute accent, in original.]

>  <b>EADDY</b> Long schooners of steamed beer, and various small mugs of `Tom and Jerry' <i>(1933,Hull Down,163</i>)

>  <b>NEWTON</b> A few West Coast `schooners' (extra long glasses) of beer. <i>(1947,Wayleggo,41</i>)

>  The name `Greymouth Schooner' is not the name of a ship but the designation given to a drinking vessel which is supposed to have a capacity of an imperial pint, or 20 ounces- double the size of the ordinary glass. West Coasters are inordinately proud of their reputation of being able to consume more beer in any given time than those in less favoured parts of the Dominion and support for their contention was forthcoming in the glass that was famed in many a story of the early Coast days as the `Greymouth Schooner' These have almost disappeared from the West Coast hostelries but one has been secured through the generosity of Mr. H.E. Wedde of Oamaru, for the Otago museum. The Museum boasts a particularly fine collection of glassware going back to the days of the early Egyptians and the Director, Dr H.E. Skinner seemed overjoyed that such a famed drinking measure as the `Greymouth Schooner' should find a place in such select company. The claim that the glass provided a full 20 ounces is disputed by Dr Skinner however, who finds that it is only [?] 17.5 ounces. <i>(Nov 22, 1950,Wayleggo</i>) [NOTES: 1950 (? 51 ? 52) Evening Star (Dunedin) ca Nov 22; or Feb 23-25; or Feb 15 (R.Mason)]

>  <b>CRUMP</b> He had already got into his stride and drank a schooner to each of Scrubby's and Sam's eight-ounce beers [in the West Coast pub]. <i>(1962,One of Us,168</i>)

>  <i> n.</i> a measure of beer; a long drink. <i>(1966,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Whitcombe's),624</i>)

>  <i> schooner ... n.</i> measure of beer, long drink. <i>(1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),17</i>)

>  <b>HULME</b> She settles on stout, opening a couple of bottles with her knife, ... She pours a schooner full, and settles back on the sheepskins. She ... pours him a drink. A twelve-ounce schooner should stop you, my lad. <i>(1983,Bone People, The,27</i>)

>  <b>BENTLEY & FRASER</b> In a back bar at Eketahuna/ They drink rum from a gigantic schooner/ <i>(1985,Grand Limerick Tour, A,[No.] 50</i>)

>  <b>GUSTAFSON</b> Although friendly with many journalists, with whom he would often have `a great `schooner' of beer' in the press bar in Bellamy's, Savage disliked many of the papers for which they worked. <i>(1986,Cradle to Grave,230</i>)

>  <b>McGILL</b> <i>schooner</i> 12 ounce glass of beer once popular particularly on West Coast. <i>(1988,Dictionary of Kiwi Slang, A,97</i>)

### scotia

 
<i>noun</i>. a (usually concave) moulding between a wall and a ceiling.

[NOTES: Jim Cameron writes: NSOD, Collins and Chambers define <i>scotia</i> as a concave/hollow moulding, esp. at the base of an (ionic) column. The OED definition is "a hollow moulding = casement". The latest citation (1878) reads "another kind of base is frequent in which a bead is subsituted for the scotia". <i>Casement</i> in turn is defined in the relevant sense as "a hollow moulding, a cavetto, not exceding one quarter round". <i>Cavettos</i>, it appears, are "principally used in cornices". All this is a bit obscure, but the definitions in NSOD etc would suggest a fairly uncommon word. The ordinary NZ use is specialised though common, and familar to most homeowners - a (usually concave) moulding between a wall and a ceiling. In NZ, it is standard and as well-known as <i>skirting board</i>.]

### Scottish alley

 
<i>noun</i>.

>  <b>SUTTON-SMITH</b> Marbles had a language of its own. There were names for the marbles, the games, and all the various aspects of the play. There were terms for marbles such as `taw' or `shooter', referring to the marbles used to fire with; `dubs', `dates', `stakes', `dukes', or `changers', referring to the marbles put down to be fired at. Then there were the terms referring to particular kinds of marbles: for example, agates, aggies, aggotties, American alleys, blood alleys, bomb-squashers, bonies, bonsers, bottlies, bull's eyes, bum-squashers, cat's eyes, chinkies, connies, duckies, eggies, glassies, Greeks, milkies, molly-bars, mulley-bars [mullibars: large marbles], peelies, peewees, piss-wees, pretties, Scotties, Scottish alleys, smokies, stinkies, stonies, stripies, tom-bobblers, white alleys, and in more recent years ball-bearings, chippies, plastics, and woodies. <i>(1972,Folkgames of Children,174</i>)

### Scotty

 
<i>noun</i>. a kind of marble

>  <b>SUTTON-SMITH</b> Marbles had a language of its own. There were names for the marbles, the games, and all the various aspects of the play. There were terms for marbles such as `taw' or `shooter', referring to the marbles used to fire with; `dubs', `dates', `stakes', `dukes', or `changers', referring to the marbles put down to be fired at. Then there were the terms referring to particular kinds of marbles: for example, agates, aggies, aggotties, American alleys, blood alleys, bomb-squashers, bonies, bonsers, bottlies, bull's eyes, bum-squashers, cat's eyes, chinkies, connies, duckies, eggies, glassies, Greeks, milkies, molly-bars, mulley-bars [mullibars: large marbles], peelies, peewees, piss-wees, pretties, Scotties, Scottish alleys, smokies, stinkies, stonies, stripies, tom-bobblers, white alleys, and in more recent years ball-bearings, chippies, plastics, and woodies. <i>(1972,Folkgames of Children,174</i>)

>  <b>KEITH & M,AIN</b> Marbles were the currency of childhood and there were an astonishing number of names for them, some referring to the material or colour, others to value or function in the game. There were agates, aggies, American alleys, blood alleys, bomb-squashers, bonies, bonsers, bottlies, bull's eyes, bum-squashers, cats-eye, [sic] chinkies, connies, duckies, eggies, glassies, Greeks, milkies, mollies, peelies, peewees, pisswees, pretties, Scotties, smokies, stinkies, stonies, stripies, tom-bobblers and whities. The march of technology added ball bearings - ballies or steelies - which were unbeatable when it came to smashing an opponent's miserable glassie. World War II[roman] brought `clayeys' often imperfectly spherical they were pathetic terracotta substitutes for real marbles. <i>(1984,NZ Yesterdays,288</i>)

<i>noun</i>. an inferior whale deficient in blubber

[NOTES: OED lean person or animal 1542. 5. scrag-whale (Nth ?) =scrag-tail whale 1701: EDD. various dial. meanings all connoting residue, useless remainder, rejects. eg wood, offal of meat, small, inferior apples.]

<i>noun</i>.

<i>verb</i>. sc. flax

>  The best kind of flax was the Tihore. The native plan of preparing it was very simple. They tore out the fibres, rubbed them together in their hands to open the bundles, and removed the small tissue that remained by scraping it with their nails. The inferior kind they prepared somewhat differently. They scraped it with a shell, having sometimes previously steeped it in water to soften the skin; they then soaked it in water for from two to four days, heated it with stones while it was wet, and scraped it again, then soaked it again, and then bleached it and dried it on poles ... <i>(Jul 13, 1870,Daily Southern Cross,3</i>)

>  It is considered necessary to scrape the flax before beating it, in consequence of the coating being chiefly composed of silex, attempting to remove which merely by the process of bruizing [sic] is attended with the destruction of the fibre. <i>(Mar 3, 1841,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,2</i>)

We coax the boys regularly - a barley sugar at half past each hour, a scroggin stop on the hour. <i>(Nov 1, 2005,NZ Herald,E8</i>)

>  If any word originating in the mountain clubs deserves to be incorporated in the language it is perhaps scroggin. That mixture of raisins, sultanas, chocolate, nuts, boiled lollies, a mixture of bits and pieces of whatever one fancies, was evolved to fill the need for a sustaining, palatable, easily-carried food, one as readily available for a bite snatched in a cold, wet, momentary halt as for a welcome spell in the warmth and sun. The word seems to come from Otago but its derivation is not clear. There is a Scotch and North of England dialect word scrog which refers to stunted bushes, and if some Otago Scot had this in mind it prompts dark thoughts as to what the original comestible may have been like. Perhaps it is one of those words that have no known ancestry, that come out of the blue, such as children sometimes so happily coin. <i>(Sep 1958,Tararua,26</i>) [NOTES: 1958 Sep Ruth Mason `Track and Trail' in Tararua 26]

>  SCROGEN 1 cup peanuts 3/4 cup dried apricots 1 + 135 gram block energy chocolate 1/2 cup mixed dried fruit 1/4 cup sunflower seeds 1/2 cup coconut 2 tablespoons powdered glucose. Roast the peanuts at 180 degrees C for 10-15 minutes, or until lightly golden. Cool. Chop the apricots and chocolate coarsely. In a strong plastic bag, put the penuts, apricots, chocolate, mixed fruit, sunflower seeds, coconut and glucose. Shake to combine. Secure closed. Use as a high energy snack food. Makes about 4 cups. <i>(Jan 7, 1980,NZ Woman's Weekly,83/2</i>)

<i>verb</i>. to treat or regard a thing or idea as worthless; cancel irrevocably, write off; wipe; wash out, in racing (of a horse) `to scratch; write off' esp. exclamation: scrub it `forget (all about) it; wipe it; `it doesn't matter'.

[NOTES: [The NZ senses, if not variants of imported Austr (cf P. above) would seem to be orig. associated with, if not originated in, the racing slang: (phs cleaning the bookmaker's slate): scrubbed or scrub (a horse) to have lost; be scratched: or scratch. But the senses also parallel those of words with similar meanings: to wipe (off) (a person or thing), get wiped; wash out (sthg), a wash-out; to write off (sbdy or sthg), a write-off. The word seems noticeable after WW2, so perhaps it was popularised by NZ servicemen who may have picked it up from British Servicemen (or Australians): cf P.4. The connotation of contempt may have derived in part by association with SCRUB n and aj `poor, mean' etc, scrubby etc; and the particular uses of this in Australasia: scrub-bull; scrubber, scrub along.]]

>  <b>MORRIS</b> <i>Scrub, n</i>. country overgrown with thick bushes. Henry Kingsley's explanation (1859), that the word means shrubbery, is singularly misleading, the English word conveying an idea of smallness and order compared with the size and confusion of the Australian use. Yet he is etymologically correct, for <i>Scrobb</i> is Old English (Anglo-Saxon) for shrub; but the use had disappeared in England. <i>(1898,Austral English,405</i>)

>  <i>Scrub, n.</i> Thicket of shrubs or bushes of too low a growth to be called <i>bush</i> (q.v.). On the plains it usually grew in belts or patches. The best known components in Canterbury are Manuka, Wild Irishman, Miki-miki (of which the shepherds make walking sticks), and Moutain pine (Totara nivalis). A single plant of scrub is called a <i>bush</i>, while of course a single specimen in <i>the bush</i> is a tree. Perhaps (if the question couldn't be settled by species) ten feet would be the dividing height between <i>s</i>. and <i>b</i>. <i>(Nov 25, 1933,Press, The,15</i>) [NOTES: 1933 Acland Glossary Press 25 Nov 15]

>  <b>HILGENDORF</b> MANUKA (<i>Leptospermum scoparium</i>), also called tea tree (of which titri is an inverted corruption), or scrub, <i>tout court</i>, is a very persistent weed on much land that is surface sown, especially in the North Island. <i>(1926,Weeds of New Zealand,126,1967</i>)

>  <b>LAING& BL,ACKWELL</b> Perhaps some mention should be made here of the Scrub, as it is strange to the visitor from the Northern Hemisphere. The light underwood of the English copse or thicket is very different from the impenetrable shaggy scrub of New Zealand. <i>(1907,Plants of NZ,21,1940</i>)

### sculling/skulling

 
<i>noun</i>. a drinking game

See: scull

>  The best-known primer for this kind of activity, and indeed an integral part of the hoon-ethos itself, is the drinking game. Designed to take the monotony out of rapid, heavy drinking, the drinking game perhaps found its purest expression in the version entitled Next. Down a drink as fast as possible (commonly known as `sculling'), turn to the bloke on your left and say `Next', whereupon he does the same ... very efficient. <i>(Dec 20, 1986,Listener (New Zealand Listener),13</i>)

>  Australian Prime Minister Bob Hawke astonished students at the New England University here tonight with a display of his drinking prowess. >  Every horse has his own way of galloping, and though English trainers have a scunner upon any colt which keeps his head up, Craganour must be taken as an exception from their rule. <i>(Jun 12, 1913,Poverty Bay Herald,5</i>)

### sea ear

 
<i>noun</i>. a former name for paua

>  <b>POLACK</b> Among the piscivorous tribes, are those well known in Europe under the appellations of snapper, tench, haddocks, pollock, salmon, gurnets, john dory, hakes, bream, sword-fish, elephant-fish, diodons, pipe-fish, cod, parrot-fish, flounders, skate, cat and dog-fish, sting-rays, eels. - Among the larger tribes that sport in shoals in the vicinity of the shore, are, sperm-whales, called <i>para </i>[as-acute] <i>paraua </i>[a3-acute] (physeter macrocephalus); black whale, <i>mungu nui </i> (black physeter); right whale, <i>tohora </i> (balaena mysticetus); finback, (balaena physalis); sun-fish (diodon mola); large-lipped whale (balaena mysticetus); large-lipped whale (balaena musculus); hump-back (balaena gibbosa); shark, <i>mango </i> (squalus); hammer-head (zygaena); pilots, (scomber); flying-fish (exocaetus volitans); and an infinity of others, besides a great variety of testaceous and crustaceous fishes that almost cover the rocks under water, such as clams, muscles, oysters, crays, cuttles, limpets, wilks, gigantic muscles, a foot in length, cockles, sea-ears, sea-eggs, star-fish, mutton-fish, &c.; from the latter the pearl is procured which they insert in the eyes of their carved images and boxes. <i>(1840,Manners & Customs of the NZers,1/202 fn</i>)

>  <b>ANDERSON</b> Of other shellfish there are ten or twelve sorts such as periwinkles, wilks, limpets, and some very beautiful sea Ears and another sort that sticks to the weeds , with some other things as sea eggs, starfish ... ed. fn Periwinkles, <i>Melarhapa</i> spp. (2), and probably <i>Zediloma</i> and <i>Melagraphia</i> spp. Whelks, <i>Cominella</i> sp. (Syn. <i>Scorpaena cottoides</i> Bloch and Schn., <i>Sebastes percoides </i>Richardson, <i>Scorpaena barathri</i> Hector, and <i>Sebastodes maccullochi </i>Phillipps) ...Sea Perch <i>Scorpaenopsis cirrosus</i> (Thunberg) <i>(1956,NZ Fishes: An Identification Guide,112</i>) [NOTES: 1955 Whitley Namelist in 1956 Graham NZ Fishes 112]

>  <b>GRAHAM</b> JOHN DORY (KUPARU)<i> Zeus australis</i> Richardson <i>Ibid.</i> 180. For some obscure reason the local abundant Seaperch, or Jock Stuart, has been termed the John Dory by Otago commercial and sport fishermen and others. <i>(1956,NZ Fishes: An Identification Guide,178</i>)

>  <b>GRAHAM</b> SEAPERCH (POHUIAKAROA) JOCK STUART, HIGHLANDER, FIVEFINGER, SOLDIERFISH or SCRODDIE <i>Helicolenus papillosus</i> (Bloch and Schneider) The seaperch is a fish well known to all fishermen both sports and commercial fishermen alike, who give it quite a number of vernacular names, a few of which are as follows: Jock Stuart, Highlander, Fivefinger and Soldierfish. These names have a bearing on some distinguishing characteristic of the fish. For instance the first two names are supposed to be given on account of the colouring of the fish resembling, in some ways, the tartan of a Scot; while Fivefingers is given on account of the so-called five (really more) fingers (rays) of the pectoral fins, on which the fish has a habit of resting on the floor of the aquarium tank. The name Soldierfish is derived from the similarities of this fish to the activities of a soldier or picket on sentinel duty. I have often seen Seaperch stand or, rather, rest at attention on its pectoral fins for lengthy periods. When it did move, it moved to the right or to the left with the precision of a well-trained soldier. The name Scroddie, commonly used at the northern end of the South Island, is derived from the word Scrod which means a young Dogfish. It appears from my researches that when the early colonists first saw a small Seaperch they at once named it Scrod and later the `ie' was tacked on to make Scroddie. <i>(1956,NZ Fishes: An Identification Guide,344</i>)

### seal's ballast

 
<i>noun</i>.

>  Anyone who had ever been about old whaling and sealing stations must have seen collections of round smooth stones of various sizes but mostly about the size of cannon-balls, lying on the beach. On asking any of the `old hands' what these are, you will at once be told that they are `seal's ballast' ... You will probably be gravely told that the seal is a migratory animal, and that when it is about to take a long journey it will trim itself to exactly the proper weight for long and easy locomotion through the water. It picks up one of these stones and swallows it and goes into the water to try the effect. If it finds it requires more ballast it comes ashore again and repeats the dose. If it has too much weight .... it vomits one or two of the stones out on the beach. Hence the stones are always termed `seals' ballast' <i>(1871,TrNZI,4/417</i>) [NOTES: (Otago)]

>  <i>second cut NZ & Austral.</i> second blow made to remove badly cut fleece, inferior piece of wool resulting from this. <i>(1986,NZ Pocket Oxford Dictionary,688</i>) [NOTES: [nf. 1982 Collins Concise Eng. Dict.]]

>  <i>second cut</i>: This results when the shears are allowed to move off the sheep's skin and so into the fleece, making another blow necessary. Second cuts spoil the fleece and are said to cost the wool industry millions of dollars a year. This is because the second cut of prime wool is downgraded to the price of locks, and the main fleece brings a lower price because of its uneven staple length. <i>(1989,NZ English Newsletter,3/27</i>) [NOTES: (Wallace Shearing Glossary)]



 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a lock of wool missed by a shearer and subsequently shorn.

>  It is impossible to make a good "second cut" to the wool as with the shears, therefore the clip is longer and more valuable. <i>(Sep 9, 1899,Hawera & Normanby Star,2</i>)

>  <b>MCKEE WRIGHT</b> Mighty lot of wool you've lost! Second cuts? <i>(1897,Station Ballads,34</i>)

>  second cut: short wool that has been cut in "second cut". <i>(Feb 21, 1968,Straight Furrow,20</i>)

>  <b>MAF</b> Second cut: Wool which is cut twice during shearing when the first cut is above the base of the staple. <i>(1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,58</i>)

>  <b>McKEE WRIGHT</b> Mighty lot of wool you've lost! Second cuts? Well, that ain't my fault, you've his wrinkled hide thanks; <i>(1897,Station Ballads,34</i>) [NOTES: (`The Bloke that Ran across a Snag')]

>  <b>MACDONALD</b> The wool table, about 7ft. x 5ft., is made of battens about 1-1/2in. wide ... to permit the locks or second cuts to fall through. <i>(1915,NZ Sheepfarming,69</i>)

>  `Locks' consist mainly of short pieces of wool such as second cuts, sweepings and short wool that falls on to the table during handling. <i>(1936,Agricultural Organization in NZ,710</i>)

>  <b>BOWEN</b> Figures taken out in this country have shown that the loss to our annual wool clip by second cuts is very large, costing many hundreds of pounds (money). <i>(1955,Wool Away!,3</i>)

>  <i>Second cut</i>: (i) A blow made to remove wool which has not been cut close enough to the skin; (ii) Short wool which has been produced by second cutting. <i>(Feb 26, 1965,Listener (New Zealand Listener),15</i>) [NOTES: (H.A.L.Laing)]

>  SECOND CUT: (i) A blow made to remove wool that has been left too long in shearing. (ii) Short wool that had been cut in a `second cut'. <i>(Feb 21, 1968,Straight Furrow,20</i>)

>  <i>Second cut</i> (1) A blow made to remove wool that has been left too long in shearing. (2) Short wool that was cut in a `second cut' <i>(Feb 24, 1977,Dominion,11</i>)

>  <i>Second cut:</i> Wool which is cut twice during shearing when the first cut is above the base of the staple. These short pieces of wool are of little value. <i>(1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,58</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a group of stock left after the faster-moving leaders or first cut has been separated off. (It is possible to have a third cut.).

### second cutting

### second shearing

>  These sheep cut an average of 6lb of wool at the second shearing, and the time of growth was five months. <i>(May 22, 1880,Otago Witness,7</i>)

### seconds

[NOTES: Jim writes: Sometimes in the form <i>manufacturers' seconds</i>. This sense is recorded in Macquarie 1981 and AMO and has been long familiar to me. [me also - DEH]. The relevant NSOD definition is less specific - "goods of a quality second and inferior to the best." Collins is similar. NZPOD following POD defines seconds as "inferior goods". ### sectionist

 
<i>noun</i>.

See: cf. section

[NOTES: 1867 Richard Taylor Wanganui 7 of the [N.Z.] The holders company's land orders were called, in the infancy of the colony, `sectionists', and were thought to be great men, as they were the only possessors of the land [ca1839-40]]

>  It is perhaps not known to your readers ... that the natives here will not permit any sectionist to take possession of his land without payment for it. They allege that Mr Jerningham Wakefield either did not buy the land or did not give sufficient payment for it .... Four sectionists only have been able to settle on their land; others have attempted, but after some trouble and expense have been driven back to town .... If the Company had appointed a proper officer here to purchase the land from the natives, and see possession given to the sectionists, they might by all this time have been settled. In the meantime the settlers are condemned to inactivity. <i>(1843,Twelve Months in Wellington,26</i>) [NOTES: 1843 Wood Twelve Months in Wellington, Port Nicholson 26-27 in 1958 Miller Early Victorian NZ 57]

>  A public meeting of the inhabitants of Wanganui, was held at the Rob Roy M'Gregor Hotel, on Saturday, the 17th July, to take into consideration the circumstances of their situation as sectionists of the New Zealand Company, and unprotected subjects of Great Britain. <i>(Aug 21, 1841,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,3</i>)

>  <b>WOOD</b> Colonel Wakefield, at the last selection of land in November, promised that the New Zealand Company would return to the sectionists any amount of [27] property (under 10 l.) they might give to the natives as payment for the land. ... <i>(Apr 15, 1842,Twelve Months in Wellington,26</i>) [NOTES: Miller Early Victorian NZ 57]

>  <b>TAYLOR</b> The holders of the company's land orders were called, in the infancy of the colony, `sectionists,' and regarded as great men, being the only possessors of land. <i>(1868,Past and Present of NZ,275</i>)

### Seddonian

 
<i>adjective</i>.

>  The ordinary track of ordinary mortals is not to be pressed by Seddonian boots. <i>(Mar 12, 1880,West Coast Times,2</i>)

>  The Secretary of the Auckland branch of the Seddonian Library and Labour Federation has (according to a contemporary) been appointed Auckland manager for the Tourist Department. <i>(Feb 26, 1902,Evening Post,4</i>)

>  Lord Plunket's arrival in New Zealand was signalised by a remarkable piece of stage-management on the part of the late King Dick Seddon. Had there been any interval between the departure of Lord Ranfurly and the arrival of Lord Plunket, Chief Justice Sir Robert Stout would have been sworn in as Acting-Governor. Mr. Seddon and Sir Robert were old political rivals. "King Dick" was determined that Sir Robert should not be his "boss" even for twenty-four hours. He therefore so aranged matters that when Lord Ranfurly was steaming out of the harbour of Wellington Lord Plunket was steaming in. The episode was unique, but quite Seddonian. <i>(Feb 4, 1910,Evening Post,3</i>)

>  THE WEEKLY LEADER OF THIS WEEK, PUBLISHED TODAY, CONTAINS: <i>Original Articles on</i> .. Seddonian Taxation ... <i>(Apr 8, 1875,West Coast Times,3</i>)

>  The Exhibition at Christchurch represented about the best that New Zealand could do at the close of the constructive Seddonian period. <i>(Nov 21, 1925,NZ Truth,6</i>)

>  There is a Seddonian and Massey touch of masterfulness in the reply by Premier Forbes to a statement current in Wellington. <i>(Apr 3, 1934,Feilding Star,4</i>)

### selling a horse

 
<i>phrase</i>. a bar game to determine who in a group is to pay for drinks

[NOTES: ca1920s p.c. W.H.B. Orsman (Marlborough): similar to Hokitika Swindle.]

>  A riot occurred at an hotel about 5 p.m. yesterday, when a young man from the country entered into a game called "selling a horse," but then withdrew. <i>(Jan 7, 1909,Wanganui Herald,5</i>)

>  Another form of gambling ... is that known as `selling a horse' ... A member of the party thinks of, or writes down a number and another member starts counting, beginning at any number below ten, and the party takes it in turn to count, much as in the Army a platoon is numbered off. The member saying the number thought of or written down collects the pool. <i>(1948,Auckland Capping Book,16</i>)

>  <b>BELTON</b> The procedure is sometimes referred to as `selling a horse' Each person pools so much money and a number is written down and hidden from view. The person who writes a number down requests one of the others to start counting, commencing at any number desired, provided that it is lower than the winning number. The counting is then carried on in rotation and stops when the written number is reached. The winner then takes the pool and pays for whatever has been purchased .... <i>(1939,Outside the Law,139</i>)

>  <b>HYDE</b> `That doesn't buy our drinks,' said Sam. Another man said: `We'll sell a horse, and find out who pays.' They were selling the horse, when a big black car slid up against the kerb. A voice called: `What's the trouble, you men?' <i>(1938,Nor the Years Condemn,85</i>)

>  Another form of gambling which I view much less harshly is that known as `selling a horse.' The process is as follows. A member of the party thinks of, or writes down a number and another member starts counting, beginning at any number below ten, and the party takes it in turn to count, much as in the Army a platoon is numbered off. The member saying the number thought of or written down collects the pool. This game, though coming under the heading Games of Chance is probably the one really honest game in that category. I myself usually win it, especially in parties where there is no one with a pencil and I think of the number. <i>(1928,Auckland University Carnival Book,16</i>) [NOTES: 1928 Auckland U.C. Students' Association Souvenir Programme Revue `Tilly in the City' 16-17]

### servantgalism

 
<i>noun</i>.

>  Amazing, the words people find buried in unlikely websites. Geoff Sommerville was browsing through Papers Past last 19th-century section of the National Library's site, and chanced on servantgalism. He reports the context told him it was a term for servants who got too big for their boots. Servantgalism, and its male equivalent flunkeiana, were slang words in use in colonial Australia when servants were hard to come by. <i>Melbourne Punch</i> in 1861, for instance, ran a cartoon of a prospective employer offering to drown a few of his children to accommodate a maid who found looking after seven would be too much. <i>(May 25, 2002,Dominion,14</i>)

>  <b>BENNETT</b> `I'm set' is ... a variant of the widespread `all set' - to be distinguished from the same phrase used in some Southern English dialects with the ... meaning ... `I'm stuck' <i>(1943,English as it is spoken in NZ,90</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. a (solid) foundation (for a timber-jack)

>  <b>REED</b> In bullocking, if a log became stuck while being drawn out of the bush, a good `set' - a solid foundation for the toes - would be obtained for the jack .... <i>Ibid.</i> 175 Great skill was required in obtaining a good `set', both with the jaws which penetrated the log, and the toes which must have a firm foundation. <i>Ibid </i>186 (R. Ross) Simmie Simmons had a set with his jack to try to hold that cat from shooting back ... . <i>(1953,Story of the Kauri, The,176</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. a seed potato, or part, for planting



 
<i>noun</i>. a dislike; prejudice espec have a set on, against, to have a down on, a prejudice against (often used adverbially: have a person set)

>  The feeling is growing here that the Wellington officials have a "set" against the Otago men, and this is given colour to by the fact that the selected sculler, Chapman, being unable to go, they have communicated with M'Cormack and passed over M'Grath. <i>(Apr 16, 1896,Evening Post,2</i>)

>  `There's two girls go to the Kaiapoi. They've got to go clean and tidy, or the other girls will have a set on them.' <i>(Apr 2, 1910,NZ Truth,249/6/1</i>)

>  <b>BENNETT</b> `To have a set on or against someone' represents a conflation of the old-established `to have a down on' and the Australian `to have (a person) set'. <i>(1943,English as it is spoken in NZ,90</i>)

>  <i>to set someone, to have a set on</i> (phrase) intend to do harm to a person. <i>(1966,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Whitcombe's),624</i>)

>  <i>have a set on NZ & Austral.</i> have a grudge against <i>(1986,NZ Pocket Oxford Dictionary,699</i>) [NOTES: [nf. 1982 Collins Concise Eng. Dict.]]



 
<i>noun</i>.

>  <b>McCARTHY</b> They were all good miners ... I was bogging the stone, Herbert was getting ready to bore the face again while Jimmy and Jack were putting up the set, that is, were timbering the walls and roof, which was necessary to prevent the walls and roof collapsing when the next `blow' took place. <i>(1973,Listen...!,52</i>)

>  <b>McARA</b> <i>Sets</i>: Basic timbering units, such as drift-sets, square-sets, shaft-sets, cribbing-sets. <i>(1978,Gold Mining at Waihi (Glossary),332</i>)

>  <b>THOMPSON</b> There was a bad flood in the mine, ... The miners at the face laboured mightily still; they were on a bonus. But the shiftmen, responsible for maintaining `sets' of timber in the mine, grew steadily more shiftless about their work while the truckers ... sat uneasily between the two extremes in alternate bursts of laziness and zeal. <i>(1980,All My Lives,61</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>.

>  <b>HARGREAVES</b> The places we put the nets out are called sets. I named one set the Three Sisters after three big cliffs down at South Head. <i>(1998,On the Next Tide,72</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>.

>  <b>MAHONEY</b> Loaded and almost ready to roll, the two bogies and their log load were called a set by the bushmen. <i>(1998,Era of the Bush Trams in NZ, The,24</i>)

>  We run out on to the main line and pick up six bogie sets, close coupled for running light. We stop at the slab heap and load up the bunker with short slabs. We also load the sets with long slabs for the two log haulers in the bush. <i>(1964,NZ Railway Observer,00</i>) [NOTES: Check page and month]



 
<i>verb</i>. to leave herd or flock to graze uninterrupted in one paddock for a long period, or in several paddocks with gates open

>  <i> Set stock</i>: To leave herd or flock to graze uninterrupted in one paddock for a long period or in several paddocks with gates <i>(1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,7</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. not to move sheep; ?to settle stock down instead of moving them

>  <b>HARTLEY</b> The system I have devised in the case of excessively strong-eyed dogs, ... gives the trainer greater command where there is likelihood of the dog `setting' sheep and failing to lift or pull. <i>(1949,Shepherd's Dogs, The,3</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. (a certain) tendency, habit

>  The observer will probably notice that [the saddle-back's] attitude is peculiar, or, in colonial phrase, `it has a queer set on it' <i>(1873,TrNZI,5/183</i>) [NOTES: (Potts)]



 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] [sp.use] [possum hunting] an elevated site on which to trap possums that is out of harm for kiwis and wekas.

>  <b>MARSHALL</b> Operators working in areas harbouring numbers of kiwis and wekas are urged to try to locate their traps on 'sets.' <i>(1984,Possum Hunting in New Zealand,42</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. [Rural] [heading dogs] to fix a sheep with a strong, concentrated fix.

>  <b>HARTLEY</b> .. in the case of excessively strong-eyed dogs, it gives the trainer greater command where there is a likelihood of the dog 'setting' sheep and failing to lift or pull. <i>(1949,Shepherd's Dogs, The,3</i>)

>  Mac again raced out on a good cast, but came in slightly at the shoulder and was inclined to set his sheep. <i>(Jul 5, 1951,NZ Farmer,33</i>)

>  <b>MILLS ET AL</b> Young strong-eyed dogs are inclined to 'set' their sheep, eyeing them in a state of frozen immobility so that they show great reluctance to move forward into the lift and pull. <i>(1964,Practical Guide to Handling Dogs and Stock,37</i>)

>  <b>NEWTON</b> Stinking with eye, Rock 'set' them about six feet from the mouth of the pen. <i>(1971,Ten Thousand Dogs,83</i>)

>  <b>NEWTON</b> Eye: common to our heading dogs. This is the action of 'setting' sheep. A very strong-eyed dog ('stinking with eye') works sheep in a manner similar to a cat stalking a bird. <i>(1971,Ten Thousand Dogs,168</i>)

<i>phrase</i>. to get something started (also as set it alight! get a move on!, hurry up!

>   <i>(1946,Johnny Enzed in the Middle East,31</i>) [NOTES: [see quot hoop it along]]

>  <b>NEWTON</b> <i>Set alight</i>: A slang term referring to the act of starting a dog on its run. <i>(1971,Ten Thousand Dogs,169</i>)

### set in

 
<i>verb</i>. to get settled into, or occupy, a claim

[NOTES: goldmining]

>  I know of one instance of a party..who "setting in" promiscuously on the beach, about three miles from Greymouth, divided GBP198 after a week's work. <i>(Jan 4, 1866,Evening Post,No. 283 : 2</i>)

>  <b>ROCHFORT</b> Our first hole, where we `set in', produced more than a pound of gold. <i>(1853,Adventures of a Surveyor,64</i>)

>  A party of four men .... who, `setting in' promiscuously on the beach ... divided 198 pounds after a week's work. <i>(1866,Evening Post,1/283/2</i>)

>  <b>PYKE</b> Here they halted, and proceeded first to encamp, then to explore the diggings and make necessary enquiries for a likely place `to set in' <i>(1873,Wild Will Enderby,Bk I ch iii 15</i>)

>  <b>McPHERSON</b> They duly pegged off and `set in' on a piece of ground where nobody supposed they would get the colour. .... They shifted their pegs and again `set in' <i>(1892,Gully Wardon,14</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. v.i. to meet and keep company

>  <b>O'REGAN</b> I mind how first we two set in. <i>(1894,Voices of Wave and Tree,14</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. of whales, to bays for calving

>  <b>BELL</b> The black whales visit the bays and coasts of New Zealand for calving, and begin to set in about the beginning of April and remain till about the beginning of September. <i>(1831,Letter</i>) [NOTES: 1831 Nov Bell Letter in 1913 McNab Old Whaling Days 3]

### set in a crack

 
<i>phrase</i>.

>  <b>PARTRIDGE</b> [The] following [was] employed by those who served in the [Great] War ... set in a crack, to settle (a matter) quickly; <i>(1935,Slang Today,286</i>)

>  <b>PARTRIDGE</b> <i>Set</i> (something)<i> in a crack</i>. To settle (a matter) quickly; e.g. <i>set a bet in a crack</i>, to wager smartly at two-up; <i>be set in a crack</i>, (of persons) to be comfortably placed (lit. or fig.), to be very pleased with circumstances: New Zealanders': from the 1890's. Perhaps ex. the idea of doing a thing as sharply as the crack of a whip. <i>(1937,Dictionary of Slang,746</i>)

>  <b>McGILL</b> <i>set in a crack</i> to settle something quickly, perhaps a wager in two-up, or to be well off or fortunate; Partridge suggests it might be from the notion of doing something as smartly as a whip is cracked; c.1890s. <i>(1988,Dictionary of Kiwi Slang, A,98</i>)
