### set-stock

 
<i>verb</i>. [Rural] to graze stock in the same location all season.

>  The dry stock are set-stocked in one or two paddocks, except when they are brought in to clean up after the herd in its grazing rotation. <i>(Feb 1, 1954,NZ Dairy Exporter,12</i>)

>  The flock is set-stocked at tupping time ... <i>(Sep 28, 1961,NZ Farmer,3</i>)

>  Ewes and lambs are set-stocked from lambing until weaning. Ewe lambs are then rotationally grazed until mid-May when they go on to kale. <i>(Jan 1965,NZ Journal of Agriculture,45</i>)

>  Now why does Dave Watt set-stock his milkers rather than graze them rotationally? <i>(Jan 13, 1977,NZ Farmer,4</i>)

>  Hinds are set-stocked or mob-stocked over winter at about 10 to the acre. <i>(1899,NZ Deer Farmer,Summer 8/3</i>)

>  <b>GORDON</b> The ewes are set-stocked, put in paddocks at 2.2 and 2.6 an acre, depending on their age and the class of country ... <i>(1987,People, Places & Paddocks,60</i>)

>  <b>RENNIE</b> Previously animals were set-stocked all year. <i>(1988,Agriculture in NZ,30</i>)

>  Ewes and cows are rotationally grazed together but separated and set stocked during lambing and calving. <i>(Sep 16, 1999,Taranaki Daily News,14</i>)

>  Cattle are set-stocked in the winter at the back of the farm so we have to buy cattle that are used to the terrain. <i>(Mar 29, 2001,Taranaki Daily News,17</i>)

>  Farm Management Spread animals widely if you are set-stocking. <i>(Feb 10, 2002,RD1.com</i>)

### set-stocked

 
<i>adjective</i>. [Rural] [of stock] grazed in one location all year or all season.

>  Set-stocked cows in a Ruakura trial are more relaxed than those on rotational grazing. <i>(Feb 1990,NZ Dairy Exporter,10</i>)

>  Set stocked lambs can increase in live weight by 8%. <i>(Jun 1, 1994,NZ Farmer,23</i>)

>  Set-stocked lambs may need cattle added to their paddocks to reduce the pasture mass. <i>(Jun 1997,AgFact,No 182</i>)

>  It can be diffcult to realise your feed surplus during spring if ewes and lambs are set-stocked. [set stocked] <i>(Nov 22, 2001,Fencepost.com,Expert farming</i>)

>  They are usually old family farms, mortgage-free, and what is called `set-stocked', i.e., not intensively grazed paddock by paddock. <i>(Dec 1952,Here & Now,50</i>)

### set-stocking

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] grazing of the same stock in the same location all year round.

>  <b>STEVENS</b> During the last thirty years two methods of grazing management have been adopted. The first and oldest is 'set-stocking.' In some areas cattle will be carried as a floating grazing unit or 'set-stocked' to deal with surplus growth. <i>(1958,Sheep.  Part 1, Sheep husbandry,59</i>)

>  <b>STEVENS</b> Set-stocking allowed the ewes to become too fat at times of the year.. The most satisfactory solution appears to be a compromise between the two systems, using set-stocking from lambing to weaning, and controlled rotational grazing during the summer, autumn and winter. <i>(1958,Sheep.  Part 1, Sheep husbandry,61</i>)

>  Set stocking is the opposite method [to mob stocking or rotational grazing] used quite commonly on hill country, where the stock is spread out over the whole farm, or most of it, the individual paddocks grazed continuously. <i>(Apr 2, 1959,NZ Farmer,15</i>)

>  .. the smallest-leaf cultivar (tahora) outyielded the larger-leafed pitau and kopu under set-stocking. <i>(Nov 1987,NZ Dairy Exporter,55</i>)

>  <i>set stocking NZ & Austral</i>. grazing of livestock in one or more paddocks for a continuous period of time (cf. <i>mob stocking</i>); <i>(1986,NZ Pocket Oxford Dictionary,699</i>)

### settlement

 
<i>noun</i>.

[NOTES: Also village settlement report]

>  <b>ELDER</b> In drawing up these drastic regulations, it is plain, Marsden practically confessed, that `the settlement system,' which depended upon the missionaries growing enough to support themselves, had failed. <i>(1932,Letters & Journals of Samuel Marsden,412 ed. fn</i>)

>  <b>WAKEFIELD</b> But I am satisfied ... that the more and greater settlements there are in New Zealand ... the better for the Wellingtonians. <i>(Jan 8, 1840,Letter</i>) [NOTES: 1840 E.G. WAKEFIELD Letter Jan 8 in 1901 FAWCETT Sir William Molesworth 173]

>  NO. I, a Specimen Number of the NEW ZEALAND GAZETTE, a Newspaper for the First and Principal Settlement of the New Zealand Land Company, which it is supposed will be at <i>Port Nicholson</i>, in <i>Cook's Straits</i>, is now presented to the public. <i>(Aug 21, 1839,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,1</i>)

>  With the passing of nearly three-quarters of a century since the venturesome pioneers commenced to push their way into the unexplored portions of Southland and laid the foundations of that settlement which has resulted in the largely cultivated province of to-day, it cannot be expected that a great many of these hardy explorers will remain much longer with us and the death of any one of them makes an irreplacable [sic] blank in a band of people which has called for the respect and admiration of the generations who have succeeded them. <i>(Nov 8, 1932,Otautau Standard & Wallace County Chronicle,3</i>)

>  The Bill provides that all moneys [sic] received on account of the purchase of the freehold of settlement lands (i.e., Land for Settlements holdings) is to be paid into the Land for Settlements Account, when it will automatically be devoted to the acquisition of further areas of private land for closer settlement. <i>(Sep 7, 1910,Evening Post,7</i>)

>  LETTERS RECEIVED .. "W.J.," on Our Frontier Settlements and Rifle Practice" .. Mr. R. McEwen, on Pollok Settlement Highway Board ... <i>(Jun 16, 1871,Daily Southern Cross,2</i>)

>  Amended regulations for village special settlement on perpetual leases, is gazetted. <i>(Jun 4, 1886,West Coast Times,4</i>)

### settler

 
<i>noun</i>. a var iety of mullet

>  This variety of mullet [which feeds in the ocean and shoals along the coast] is known to the fishermen and the [Northland] settlers as the `clean-gut', `clean-run', or `sea-mullet'. ... The other variety [which stays in the harbour] is known to the fishermen as the `settler' or muddy fish'. When opened they are not clean and bright ... but full of slimy mud ... <i>Ibid.</i> 7 The fishermen in Kaipara distinguish between `school fish' and `settlers'. ... The `settlers' are those mullet of moderate size which stay in the harbour and run up rivers. <i>(1897,AJHR,H-17/2</i>) [NOTES: Hector Protection of Mullet]



 
<i>noun</i>. an immigrant who set up home in NZ, cf. early settler

>  We would also draw your Honor's attention to the fact that the Government reserve near the mouth of the Kaitangata Creek is admirably suited for the site of a Jetty, having natural facilities nowhere else to be found in the district, and being near the proposed Railway Station will thus enable up-country settlers to forward or receive goods with the least possible delay ... <i>(Jan 30, 1874,Bruce Herald,4</i>)

>  The above results are due largely to the great intrinsic worth of the country which the new settlers adopted as their home, but they are also due to the sturdy, industrious, and upright character of the men who came out from Scotland in the John Wickliffe, Philip Laing, and other vessels to form a Scottish settlement in the New World. <i>(Mar 23, 1898,Poverty Bay Herald,2</i>)

>  It appears that the Times had again opened its columns to assailants of the Port Nicholson settlers, and had lent its influence to bolster up the tottering clique at Auckland. <i>(Feb 26, 1842,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,2</i>)

<i>noun</i>. a farmer

<i>noun</i>. .

There is no evidence of such games before 1900, but a number of instances between 1900 and 1920 are recorded. The games were known as Fives, Tens, Sevens, and Walls and have been recorded more often since under the names O'Leary or Sevens. ### shagroon

 
<i>noun</i>. an immigrant esp. from Australia, but also from other settlements) to the early Canterbury settlement, often applied to one settled there before the main influx of PILGRIMS (contrast PILGRIM, PRE-ADAMITE, PROPHET)

[NOTES: History: an early non-Canterbury Association settler in Canterbury. (hist) [OED2 (following Morris) Phs f. Irish <i>seachra'n </i>wandering.:<i> searchan</i> transliterates <i>shaughraun </i>=?/sh |r n/: I have not been able to find Walls's<i> shabberoon</i>, etc., but if these forms exist they are more likely to be alterations of <i>shagroon</i> towards a play on<i> shab</i>, a common English dialect variant of <i>scab</i>, the dread sheep disease of early NZ, which would fit in with the usu.derogatory or dismissive connotations of the word.b But <i>shab, shabbaroon </i>are not yet otherwise attested in NZ contexts and must be ruled out; as must Sinclair's suggestion of <i>shagreen</i> (rough exterior) spg also <i>shagaroon, shagrun;</i> ?erron. spg or misprint <i>shaproon</i>; cf Walls's <i>shabberoon etc</i>. occas. cap. Morris 1898]

>  In a letter dated 8th March 1850, in mentioning a visit to the Taieri Plain, the writer says: "We visited the warri or hut of a Shaproon - <i>ie.,</i> one of the retired whalers 'who have married Maori wives.' Can you tell me the meaning and derivation of the word Shaproon, and why the retired whalers were so called?" <i>Ibid</i> 22 September. 24   Shaproon is from the French <i>chaperon</i>, and originally meant "little captain." ..There is no doubt that the term was used by French sailors and those in contact with them with the same meaning as English sailors use the word mate. Mispronounced and misspelt by its adoption into the English of rough-and-ready sea-faring men, shaproon would have this signification, and even under certain circumstances might reassume its original acceptation of little leader, and be addressed to the captain of a small band, and become equivalent in a new country, as this was 50 years ago, to the word pioneer. <i>(Sep 15, 1892,Otago Witness,24</i>)

>  <b>PARTRIDGE</b> <i>Shagroons.</i> Australian settlers that went<i> en masse</i>, to Canterbury, New Zealand, in 1851-2: Australian and New Zealand: ca. 1851-70. B., 1942. With a pun on <i>shagreen</i>, the rough skin of<i> sharks. </i> <i>(1949,Dictionary of Slang Addenda,1165</i>)

The following was written in reply:] `Dream of Shagroon' [title] I saw men of another aspect arrive at the pilgrim-land. ... The Pilgrims looked with contemptuous eye on this people of strange aspect and impure blood, and did despise them. ... I awoke - and lo! the land which was to have been sacred to the orthodox foot only of a `body of English gentlemen', was in possession of the `stragglers, the whalers, and the stock-drivers from other settlements'. Alas! for the goodly land, - the land of the Canterbury Pilgrims. <i>(May 7, 1851,NZ Spectator</i>) [NOTES: 1851 May 7 NZ Spectator and Cook's Strait Guardian (Wellington) in 1947 Reed Story of Canterbury 111 [1851]

>  <b>WALL</b> Who first called these immigrants by this opprobrious name is not stated, but it seems to me most probable that the Pilgrims used it as a term of contempt, and [110] that the immigrants took it to themselves much as the `Old Contemptibles' ... adopted their enemies' names in a spirit of defiance. ... There arises the further question as to the origin of the word which ... has been explained as an Irish `shaughraun'. Now why should an Irish word have been used at that time by the English settlers in Canterbury? ... My belief is that the word was not originally `Shagroon' but `Shabroon', `shabberoon', `shabbaroon' (all spellings occur) which is on record from the 18th century onwards, meaning `a mean, shabby fellow', `a disreputable or mean-spirited fellow', and this, which would be probably familiar to the English Pilgrims, is just the sort of term which would naturally be used to describe their rivals. This `shabroon' derives from the slang `shab', a low fellow, recorded as early as 1637, and no doubt closely alied to the standard `shabby', and ultimately from `shab' and `scab', two forms of the old English word. ... I conjecture that the `shabroon' [?does Wall mean `shagroon] of the English Pilgrims was by some pronounced with the `b' and by others with the `g', nobody ever having seen the word written or printed. [EDD records only `shaggareen' from east Yorkshire `an untidy, slovenly person'; possibly f. shabrag] <i>(Nov 25, 1948,Letter</i>) [NOTES: 1948 Nov 25 Arnold Wall letter in 1947 Reed Story of Canterbury 109-110]

>  <b>REED</b> It appears to have been the Australian squatters [let in to Canterbury by Godley to provide capital and flocks for unsold land] who jocularly termed the pioneer English settlers the `Canterbury Pilgrims', ... The Australian squatters were dubbed `Shagroons', a term the origin of which appears to be somewhat elusive. [Quotes Webster and Funk and Wagnall: both definitions erroneous] <i>(1947,Story of Canterbury, The,109</i>)

>  <i>Shagroon.</i>- The Australian squatters who invaded Canterbury in 1851-(2) We probably owe most of the Australian sheep farming terms and practice we have here to them. They always spoke of coming down (not over) from Australia. They were also called<i> prophets</i>(q.v.). (C.R., p. 8; [1898 Morris Austral-English], which derives ss. from Irish <i>Shaughraun</i>.) <i>(Nov 25, 1933,Press, The,15</i>) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]

>  <b>MORRIS</b> When the province of Canterbury, in New Zealand, was first settled, the men who came from England were called <i>Pilgrims</i>, all others<i>Shagroons</i>, probably a modification of the Irish word <i>Shaughraun. </i> <i>(1898,Austral English,410</i>)

>  <i>shagroon n.</i> a name once used in part of New Zealand for a settler from some other country than England. [origin uncertain] <i>(1929,Whitcombe's Etym. Dict. Aust-NZ Suppl.,10</i>)

>  <b>THOMSON</b> ...An old Australian squatter, who visited the Canterbury settlement in 1851, divided the inhabitants into pilgrims, shagruns, and prophets; the first were the original colonists, the second were people from other parts of New Zealand, and the last were settlers from Australia. <i>(1859,Story of New Zealand, The,186</i>)

>  The pilgrim toiled for his crop. ... Shortly the pilgrim and prophet agreed The plough and the crook couldn't live far apart. <i>(1866,Canterbury Rhymes</i>) [NOTES: [1851] 1866 Canterbury Rhymes 5, 9, 125 `Pilgrims and Prophets'. [title of Poem] 9.[NOTE 1866] 125. During the first year of the Settlement, Canterbury was invaded by a body of sheep-farmers from Port Philip (Victoria) who were regarded by the settlers partly with admiration as successful Colonists, and partly with horror as disbelievers in the art of colonisation and the `Canterbury System'. The visitors found the country admirably adapted for sheep-farming, and they treated with some contempt the raw emigrants from England who looked to agriculture as the foundation of their fortunes. One of the vistiors, who seem to have delighted in the soubriquet of `Shagroon', ventured to prophesy, in a letter, which found its way into print, that the `Canterbury Pilgrims' would soon be ruined and their country left for occupation by his more enlightened comrades. The `pilgrims' sought no harsher revenge than to nickname their Port Philip visitors `prophets' and to take example from their experience in pastoral pursuits. The Canterbury pasturage system was quickly adapted to the requirements of sheepfarming on a large scale, and `pilgrims' and `prophets' were soon merged into one class of Canterbury runholders.]

>  <b>PRATT</b> In the `Dream of a Shagroon' which bore the date Ko Motinau, April 1851, and which first appeared in the `Wellington Spectator' of May 7th, the term Pilgrim was first applied to the settlers; it was also predicted in it that the `Pilgrims', would be `smashed' and the `Shagroons' left in undisputed possession of the country for their flocks and herds. <i>(1877,Colonial Experiences,234</i>)

This was carried out principally by stock owners from Australia, who, to distinguish them from the Pilgrims or those who came from England direct to Canterbury, were called Shagroons. What this title is derived from is not quite clear. An amusing piece ... respecting the climate of New Zealand, and particularly Canterbury, was published about this time, and as it shews what opinion our Australian visitors held of our vaunted New Zealand climate, perhaps to reproduce it would be interesting. ... our Australian bard, under the title of `The Shagroon's Lament,' discourses as follows:- <i>(1886,Stray Leaves,10</i>)

The Canterbury Association settlers were `Pilgrims', while those established in Canterbury before their arrival were `pre-Adamites' <i>(1900,Canterbury Old & New,109</i>)

### shaker

 
<i>noun</i>.

>  <b>CARR</b> When the flax arrives at the mill it is weighed and credited to the cutter. The `bench loader' then takes two or three bundles and puts them in a barrel (heavy end down). He then takes the longest leaves and places them on a bench convenient to the `feeder'. ...[44] The `feeder' takes each blade separately and places the butt end into the `stripper' which takes the green outer covering off. ... The fibre as it leaves the stripper is caught by the `fly boy', who collects enough to make into a hank, which he places convenient for the `shaker'. The latter, with a motion like cracking a whip, gets rid of as much rubbish as possible, after which he places the hank handy for the `washer'. This man places the fibre in a vat, through which ... clean water is running. <i>(1913,Country Work,43</i>)

### shanty

 
<i>noun</i>. [obsolete] a small, wayside public house or inn, mainly unlicensed and often rough-and-ready; a grog-shop; a low-class ACCOMMODATION HOUSE

See: cf. grog-shanty

>  "A miserable shanty with six bare rooms." This was how Mr. R. A. Wright described a certain hotel in Wellington in the House last night, when defending Mr. T. E. Taylor's proposal for an increase of 25 per cent. in the excise duty on beer. <i>(Nov 24, 1909,Taranaki Herald,3</i>)

>  <b>POWER</b> We had heard that a `pakeha' had built a shanty on the opposite side of the river for the purpose of entertaining travellers, and ferrying them across. <i>(Apr 1848,Sketches in NZ,168,1849</i>)

>  <b>HARPER</b> There happened to be at the foot of the hill a little wooden shanty where refreshments were on sale. <i>(Dec 25, 1856,Letters from Canterbury, NZ,10,1914</i>)

>  <b>HARPER</b> Some shanty of a public house .... <i>(Jul 20, 1861,Letters from Canterbury, NZ,1914</i>)

>  Every four or five miles on the road an accommodation house is met. These .... are not mere `shanties', and the traveller, with ordinary precautions, is always safe. <i>(1862,Otago: Its Goldfields and Resources,28</i>)

>  There are only four shanties in Havelock. <i>(1864,Saturday Review,79</i>)

>  We then went up to the Greenstone junction [West Coast] and stoped at a shanty, that is a calico house where everything is sold, principally grog. <i>(Apr 29, 1865,Chudleigh Diary,179,1950</i>)

>  <b>BURGESS</b> While we were at the township [in Otago, c1862 March], one of our acquaintances came to me and told me there was a man in a disreputable shanty, that had plenty of money and would I come and put him up? Now the Wetherstone diggings were very quiet, so that I objected to men being put up and let go to alarm the place - for I anticipated robbing this banker sooner or later, and that would do me. <i>(1866,Confessions,76,1983</i>)

>  <b>HARPER</b> ... we pull up at a little shanty for a welcome lunch. <i>(Oct 15, 1866,Letters from Canterbury, NZ,96,1914</i>) [NOTES: [?wayside inn]]

>  <b>THOMSON</b> A fine two story hotel now stands on the site of our lodgings for that night ....... and mine host, now grown stout with prosperity, recounts his various experiences in the old shanty <i>(1867,Rambles with a Philosopher,48</i>)

>  <b>HARPER</b> Accordingly, such rough accommodation as the small shanty of an hotel [near Otira] could ive us, ... was our portion for the night. <i>(Jul 10, 1868,Letters from Canterbury, NZ,129,1914</i>)

>  He kept a shanty at Otago <i>(1869,Punch or the Auckland Charivari,162</i>)

>  <b>MONEY</b> Here were canvas and galvanised iron stoves, public houses, restaurants, shanties of all descriptions, and with every conceivable name, scattered around in all directions; ... <i>Ibid.</i> 83 ... I walked back a distance of eight miles ... to a small wayside shanty, close to a narrow belt of bush ... The landlord was a digger ... cp <i>shanty</i> (rough pub) and <i>inn </i>... ... the landlord ... asked me if I had searched the bush track leading from his shanty to the inn from whence I had started. <i>(1871,Knocking About in NZ,9</i>)

>  <b>CAIRD</b> Shanty or small public house. <i>(1874,NZ Sheepfarming,9</i>)

>  Thus, recently, a merry party of four recruits in the police force set out to try to trap a sly-grog shanty. <i>(May 3, 1919,NZ Truth,4</i>)

>  About 10 o'clock George Rook came to the house and invited him to go down to the shanty, where he and some of his cobbers were endeavoring - in the local colloquialism - to give a five-gallon jar of beer "a terrible thrashing." <i>(May 19, 1927,NZ Truth,3</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. (formerly) a rough, country inn, or a place selling sly grog.

[NOTES: >1875. `Spectator' (Melbourne), June 26, p. 91, col. I]

>  <b>BATHGATE</b> Some of the keepers of the shanties in the interior of the North Island, which they dignify with the name of hotels, ...[get] the maoris to run up a long score for liquor and then secure a mortgage over their lands. <i>(1880,New Zealand (various authors/titles),99</i>)

[in Westport] I should have said canvas `shanties'. At these places of refreshment grog was retailed at the small charge of one shilling per `nobbler'. <i>(1881,Chequered Career,60</i>)

>  From a play review. The doctor is keeping a shanty, at which the dispenser is drinking himself to death. <i>(Feb 10, 1890,Evening Star</i>)

>  <b>MORRIS</b> <i>Shanty, n</i>. (1) a hastily erected wooden house; (2) a public-house, especially unlicensed: a sly-grog shop. The word is by origin Keltic (Irish). In the first sense, its use is Canadian or American; in the last, Australian. In Barrere and Leland it is said that circus and showmen always call a public-house a shanty. <i>(1898,Austral English,411</i>)

>  <i>Shan&#769;.ty </i>(sh&abreve.n&#769;.t&ybreve.),<i> n. [Add.]</i> 2. A small inn in the Australian bush; - public house in a bush township. <i>(1898,Merriam-Webster Third International,2031</i>)

>  <i> ~ n</i>. a public-house, esp. an unlicensed one;-v.i. to frequent shanties. -shant'y-keeper n. <i>(1929,Whitcombe's Etym. Dict. Aust-NZ Suppl.,10</i>)

>  <b>PINFOLD</b> The lodging places of the pioneer parson were many and various. ... His first `breaking in' was to be given a `shake-down' under the counter of the public house; a small rude wooden `shanty' that has been hurriedly erected. <i>(1930,Fifty Years In Maoriland,66</i>)

Truly, this pubbery was just short of shanty, typical of the `Outer Barcoo', but where Maories, their Wahines, or broken down `Remittancers' could drown their sorrows, wander into the `arms of Bacchus' or chase pink elephants. <i>(1960,Memories of Maoriland,157</i>)

>  <b>LEE</b> Don't blame the Colonial Government,/ If your children lack for bread -/ But blame the wayside shanty/ For the reckless life you've led./ <i>(1964,Shiner Slattery,9</i>)

>  <i> ~ n.</i> small public house, especially if unlicensed; sly grogshop, whence shanty-keeper, the publican; a small but-like dwelling. <i>(1966,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Whitcombe's),624</i>)

>  <b>MAY</b> Duffer rushes collapsed so quickly that storekeepers could find themselves in the back-of-beyond with a fully-stocked shanty and no sales to pay for the cost of packing-in and packing-out. <i>(1967,West Coast Gold Rushes,281,1962</i>)

>  <i> shanty ... n</i>. small public house, especially if unlicensed; sly grogshop; whence <i>shanty-keeper</i>, the publican; small hut-like dwelling. <i>(1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),17</i>)

>  <b>HARPER</b> Pubs provided liquor and accommodation, even if the accommodation had to be on the floor; shanties provided just liquor. <i>(1975,Eight Daughters,20</i>)

>  <i> shanty ...2. Austral. & N.Z. </i>a public house, esp. an unlicensed one. <i>(1982,Collins Concise English Dictionary,1060</i>) [NOTES: [nf. 1986 NZPOD; 1985 Collins NZ Compact Dict. 446]]



 
<i>noun</i>. a rough wooden hut or shack, often in the bush

See: cf. bush shanty

>  A TYPICAL NORTH ISLAND BUSH SHANTY. <i>(Dec 19, 1906,Otago Witness,15</i>) [NOTES: Photo Caption]

>  Virtually every settlement in the youngcolony originally clustered around itstaverns - even if they were only tatteredcalico shanties. <i>(Jan 12, 1985,Listener (New Zealand Listener),26</i>)

>  Kororarika is still the principal settlement, and contains about [296] twenty houses, ... and many shanties, besides tents. It is chiefly inhabited by the lowest order of vagabonds, mostly runaway sailors and convicts, and is appropriately named `Blackguard Beach'. <i>(1852,U.S. Exploring Expedition,1/295-296</i>) [NOTES: 1840 Mar in 1852 Wilkes U.S. Exploring Expedition]

>  <b>HAY</b> There are shanties and shanties. It is necessary to explain. Primarily, in its Canadian and original sense, the term means a log-house - a hut made of rough squared logs, built up upon each other. Such log-huts are not common in this country, though they may be seen here and there. ... The native whare[e-grave] of thatch is quickly and easily raised, serves all requirements, and lasts for years ... A shanty here, is a name applied to almost any kind of nondescript erection, which would not come under the designation of [117] whare[e-grave], or be honoured by the ambitious title of house. Rough edifices of planking are the common form. a hut (cf <i>built a warre </i>Jan 6) <i>(1882,Brighter Britain,1/116</i>)

>  <b>BEATTIE</b> He [the pioneer pastoralist] has built a domicile of some sort, be it of canvas, calico, bagging, sticks, ferntrees, grass, slabs, mud, clay, stone, or wattle and daub. He may call it various names according to its materials, but three names would not enter his head - i.e., crib, bach, or shack. He may call it a cabin, a shanty, a cottage, a warrie [whare], but probably he would use the commonest term of all - hut. <i>(1947,Early Runholding in Otago,38</i>)

>  <b>REED</b> A shattered site having been selected near to running water, an advance party would be sent to clear the necessary space and build a `shanty' which, in the earlier days, served inclusively as dormitory, dining hall and cookhouse. 1953 <i>op.cit.</i> 142 (Mrs. Brown's account) On our first arrival at a new camp we generally lived in a nikau whare until my husband could split the palings and build a shanty for us; the men lived in another and larger shanty. <i>(1953,Story of the Kauri, The,130</i>)

>  Built a shanty at the creek. [He uses <i>warre</i> on Jan. 6] <i>(Jan 13, 1851,Torlesse Papers,191,1958</i>)

>  <b>RIDGEWAY</b> Why a `bushman' would run up a `settler's first home' at a tithe of the expense .... his trained and ready hand runs up his hut - `shanty', or whatever you like to call it. <i>(1860,Voices from Auckland,67</i>)

>  [Dunedin's] first shanties have given place to goodly stone edifices, ... <i>(Mar 23, 1861,Otago Witness,5</i>)

>  At an inquest on Richard Benjamin Harris, who was found burnt to death after a fire in his shanty at Waitete on Sunday, the Coroner returned a verdict of accidental death. <i>(Oct 15, 1912,Evening Post,8</i>)

>  Lowe left with sheep went to Lowes shanty. <i>(Nov 29, 1862,Puketoi Station Diary</i>)

>  ... two roomed wooden shanties fetch [a pound] per <i>(1864,Saturday Review,10/120</i>) [NOTES: 1864-67 Saturday Review (Dunedin) X/120]

>  <b>MONEY</b> was much amused by a trio who arrived in the township and put up opposite my `shanty' <i>(1871,Knocking About in NZ,17</i>)

>  <b>LADY BARKER</b> We reached the little shanty [i.e. bushman's log hut] <i>(1873,Station Amusements in NZ,20</i>)

[116] ... made not less welcome the miserable `shanty' in which we took refuge <i>(1971,Mr Surveyor Thomson,115</i>) [NOTES: 1876 visit to West Coast in 1971 Hall-Jones Mr Surveyor Thomson 115, 116 (Griffiths Collection)]

>  <b>D'AVIGDOR</b> I am writing in a little frail wooden shanty, pompously called the Otira Hold. <i>(1888,Antipodean Notes,134</i>)

>  A group of what are termed `shanties' are erected [built with palings and roofed with shingles] <i>(1902,NZ Illustrated Magazine,5/372</i>) [NOTES: (`Bush Life')]

>  <b>R. MASON</b> I can remember this use in Auckland district 1931-8. Old abandoned shanties in the Waitakeres were still called by that name then. <i>(1931,Personal Communication</i>) [NOTES: ca1931-1938 R.Mason p.c.]

>  <b>SEVERINSEN</b> The night was spent at the Fohs [?] Hut, a rough, dark, musterers' shanty. <i>(1970,Hunt the Far Mountain,97</i>)

>  The tin shanty which was supposed to protect the locomotive used on haulage work from the ravages of rust and decay. <i>(Jan 30, 1930,NZ Truth,1</i>)

>  Take the sharemilker who is milking his 100 cows. He rises at half-past two a.m., and musters his cows, has to get them miked by seven o'clock, take his milk to the factory; and after that has to feed over 90 calves, and about thirty pigs. He has to provide root crops for his pigs, and see that he has a sufficient supply of hay, etc., for his cows in the winter, keep his fences in repair, and stump what ground he requires to grow his crops. There is no eight hours for that sharemilker. <i>(Mar 9, 1905,Hawera & Normanby Star,2</i>)

>  When you're playin' these Sons of the Sharemilkers, yous have to make real sure that if anythin' niffs even slightly of dried milk powder, yous knock it over, stamp on it until it stops squeakin', and then jump on it again just to make sure. <i>(Oct 18, 1998,Sunday Star Times,B3</i>)

>  As for the last verse.. it's so much thefarmhand and the sharemilker and everyoneexcept the boss that it just isn't true. <i>(1955,She'll Be Right Record Sleeve,00</i>)

>  <b>BACON</b> <i>sharemilker</i>-One who contracts to milk a herd of cows for a share of profits. In general, sharemilkers fall into three categories: first, the 29 per cent sharemilker, second, the 39 per cent man, third, the 50 per cent man. The 29 per cent man contracts to milk the farmer's herd and attend to their wants only; he helps at haymaking, etc. as part of the herd's `wants', but in general, once the cows have been attended to for the two daily milkings, his time is his own. The 39 per cent man contracts to milk the herd owned by the farmer and to do all the other general farm work. For this he receives 39 per cent of the herd profits. The 50 per cent sharemilker runs his own herd of cows on another man's land. He does all the farm work, and receives 50 per cent of the profits. Many farmers who today have their own farms in New Zealand started off as 39 per cent share milkers, saved enough to buy their own herds and so became 50 per cent milkers, then saved again to purchase land themselves (or on which they put sharemilkers!) <i>(1963,In the Sticks,183</i>)

>  A feature of dairy-farming in New Zealand has been the development of share-milking, akin to the old French system of me[acute]tayage or the sharefarming common with annual crops such as cotton in the United states of America. Under this system the owner usually provides the land, plant, and herd, while the share-milker provides labour and receives in return one-third to one-half of the gross returns. In other cases the sharemilker also provides the dairy herd and receives two-thirds of the gross receipts. <i>(1943,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,24/231a</i>)

<i>verb</i>.

>  <b>ACTON-ADAMS</b> It is courting disaster for you to attempt to muster and shear a back-country run so far from the labour market. <i>(Apr 5, 1906,Letter</i>) [NOTES: 1906 Apr 5 Acton-Adams Letter in 1969 McCaskill Molesworth 93]



 
<i>verb</i>. (a shed, a run, a mob) to complete shearing on

>  <b>BOWEN</b>  <i>(1956,Wool Away!,54</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. of a shed, run, station etc, to own sheep (?) (cf Acland 1933)

>  <i> Shear</i>.-To own [sheep]. E.g. `How many sheep have you?'- `I generally <i>s</i>. about 8000.' (C.) >  <b>NEWTON</b> Lake Coleridge Station shore 22,000. <i>(1947,Wayleggo,37</i>)

>  <b>OGONOWSKA-COATES</b> <i>Shear.</i> To cut the wool off a sheep. Also used to count the number of sheep owned - e.g., `I shear about six thousand.' <i>(1987,Boards, Blades & Barebellies,97</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. to produce (a fleece) by being shorn (cf CLIP @v)

<i>verb</i>. a. shear for the boss/ shear a few for oneself

>  <b>RICHARDS</b> Les always held to the opinion that if you did not get `chipped' at least once a day, you were shearing entirely for the boss. He [the critical foreman] failed to show any sense of humour when Les ... replied: `I shore a few for myself that run'. <i>(1986,Off the Sheep's Back,122</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. [Rural] [sp. use] [sheep farming] to own or run sheep.

>  <b>FITTON</b> The shearing of the sheep is generally done by contract; ... at so much per 100 sheep shorn - their [sc. hands'] rations, in addition to their pay, being provided for the shearers. <i>(1856,New Zealand (various authors/titles),220</i>)

>  <b>HARPER</b> Shearing ... is in full swing, so there are a number of extra men, besides the shepherds of the station, shearers, fleece-pickers, wool sorters, and `rouse-abouts'. <i>(Jul 20, 1861,Letters from Canterbury, NZ,54,1914</i>)

>  <b>BARKER</b> There were about twenty-five shearers at work ... <i>(1865,Station Life in NZ,32,1870</i>)

>  [defined in section 3 The electoral Laws Amendment Act, 1893] <i>(1894,NZ Official Yearbook,252</i>)

>  <i>Shearer</i>.- One who shears (and while so employed does nothing else). <i>Ss</i>., who always work in company and generally stick to the work for years, meet a great many people and see a great many stations; so they have a great store of expressions connected with their work. Some of them have already been noted (<i>rosella, cobbler</i>, etc.) If two <i>ss</i>. are working out of sight of each other, they can tell one another `where they are' (what part of the sheep they are on) to an inch. A shearer first shears the belly (<i>on the b</i>.), then<i> opens up</i> or goes <i>up the neck</i>, then successively does his <i>first leg, first side, up the back,</i> and so on; finally the last blows trim the <i>last leg</i>, and he is <i>off</i>. But they also use a rhyming slang sometimes among themselves; say,<i> `found a nail'</i> for <i>`round the tail', `hutch'</i> for <i>`crutch',</i> and so on. I have always meant to collect these terms but never have. (C.) <i>(Nov 25, 1933,Press, The,15</i>) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]

>  <b>RICHARDS</b> Otoro was George's first contract shed. ... But all his shed hands, shearers and his wool classer had been with him before. <i>(1986,Off the Sheep's Back,94</i>)

>  <b>OGONOWSKA-COATES</b> <i>Shearer</i>. One who shears. <i>(1987,Boards, Blades & Barebellies,97</i>)

>  <i> shearer</i>: Like other shed employees, the shearer has many names, for example, `greasy', `gouger', `stooper', `bladesman', `woolhawk', `brute' and `tiger'. <i>(1989,NZ English Newsletter,3/27</i>) [NOTES: Wallace Shearing Glossary]

### shearing blast

 
<i>noun</i>. Shearing-blast may be of two kinds. True shearing-blast is caused by the comb of the shearing-machine actually damaging the surface of the skin. This defect is seen as numerous lines parallel to each other running in various directions on the skin. The other defect [in pelts] often described as shearing-blast is really due to sunburn.

<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a woolshed area where shearing stands are located and sheep are shorn.

>  "That tenders be called for raising GBP30,000 for the purpose of immediately carrying out the following works - .. running out a wharf from the said reclamation a distance of 250 feet, and erecting shearlegs at the end thereof to lift no less than 25 tons." <i>(Jan 22, 1883,Evening Post,2</i>)

>  Fore part, people employ'd getting a spar out of the Creek for a windlass, and one for the sheer legs. At 11 A.M. took the Sheers down, and brought two legs ashore to put the cross-piece on. <i>(Oct 2, 1839,Piraki Log,99,ed. Anson 1911</i>)

>  <b>COWAN</b> Near by the foot of the old whalers' shear-legs is the place ... where Tama ... landed [from his canoe]. <i>(1926,Travel in NZ,23</i>)

>  <b>BEATTIE</b> The sheerlegs [of the shore whaling station] were still standing and whales were about. [sc to hang a carcase on] <i>(1939,First White Boy Born in Otago,53</i>)

>  From the peculiar crane-like conformation of Derrick's gibbet, all similar cranes used on shipboard were called derricks of course, and the name has even lately been transferred to ordinary "shear legs." <i>(Jan 12, 1859,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,2</i>)

>  On Monday, Thomas Oldcorn, a middle-aged carter, residing at Whangarei, was driving a five-horsed covered van between the shear legs of a derrick. <i>(Apr 22, 1915,Ashburton Guardian,5</i>)

>  Mum and me, we rigged a sheerlegs in the garden with four-by-twos and took  him [sc. the bull] to bits. <i>(Oct 15, 1965,Listener (New Zealand Listener),9</i>)

<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a sheep after its first shearing.

<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a young or novice shearer.

<i>noun</i>. a) a pair of large scissors with long, heavy blades. b) any of various cutting implements resembling scissors. c) a shearers' cry for a spell; a spell-oh

<i>noun</i>.

See: also shearlegs

>  To Wangeloar to cut spars for shears. <i>(Jan 17, 1839,Piraki Log,75,ed. Anson 1911</i>)

>  <b>BARNICOAT</b> Whale Shears <i>(1845,Journal,167</i>)

>  We made a pair of shears to lift the safe out of the boat. It worked well. <i>(Sep 20, 1877,Chudleigh Diary,263,1950</i>)

>  <b>MONRO</b> As we entered it, we passed the shears by which the whales are hoisted up in the operation of stripping them of their blubber. (Chathams) <i>(Jul 20, 1844,Notes of a Journey</i>) [NOTES: 1844 Monro Notes of a Journey (Nelson Examiner July 20 et seq.) in 1898 Hocken Contributions 240]

>  <b>TAYLOR</b> there is a large building containing about 6 large coppers with furnaces beneath which the blubber is boiled or technically speaking tryed out. ... there are three large poles erected in the sea forming a triangle which are called shears on which a platform is made and to this the whales are towed, and here cut up ... <i>(Apr 1843,Journal,15</i>)

>  <b>DIEFFENBACH</b> The tongue was of a white or ash colour, blackish towards the root. This organ gave several barrels of oil, and is a monopoly of the `tonguer,' or `cutter-in.' The latter operation is performed in Te-awa-iti near the shores, where by means of a windlass the whale is raised to the surface of the water under a scaffold called the `shears.' <i>(1843,Travels in NZ,1/51</i>)

>  <b>SHORTLAND</b> A pair of sheers, such as are used for taking out or putting in the masts of ships, must be erected [at whaling stations], in order to raise the immense carcases above water, that they may be cut up more [conveniently]. <i>(1851,Southern Districts of NZ,108</i>)

### shearwater

 
<i>noun</i>. rain-bird, wet-bird,  laughing jackass, hakoakoa

>  <b>PARKINSON</b> We saw several albatrosses, pintados, and shear-waters. Latitude 33[degree sign]35'. <i>(Aug 27, 1769,Journal</i>)

>  <b>FORSTER</b> About the Evening [in the Indian Ocean] I saw vast numbers of small Petrels, the black Puffin or Shearwater, Cape Pidgeons or Pintadas, & two kinds of Albatrosses viz the great white <i>Diomedeaa exulans;</i> & a large brown-reddish one, which I had seen before ... <i>(Nov 24, 1772,Resolution Journal of J.R. Forster, The,2/183</i>)

>  <b>FORSTER</b> We saw immense flocks of blackbanded Petrels, common & black Shearwaters, ...[ed. fn] White-chinned petrel. Forster calls this species `black petrels or shearwaters'. <i>(Feb 11, 1773,Resolution Journal of J.R. Forster, The,2/225</i>)

>  <b>MONRO</b> The cottages in Stewart's Island are all well garnished with a luxury of the southward - the mutton bird. This I take to be the bird which is sometimes called the sheerwater, or the sooty petrel - a black bird about the size of a duck, with long wings, which all of us have seen on our voyage out skimming over the waves. In the month of December these birds resort to the rocky islands about Foveaux's Straits in great numbers, for the purpose of breeding. <i>(1844,Notes of a Journey</i>) [NOTES: 1844 Monro Notes of a Journey (Nelson Examiner July 20 et seq.) in 1898 Hocken Contributions 254]

>  <b>HUTTON</b> 125. PUFFINUS GAVIUS. Forst. Rain-bird or Wet-bird. Shearwater. Laughing Jackass(?). Hakoakoa. <i>P. opisthomelas</i>. COUES. <i>P. assimilis</i>. HUTTON <i>(1871,Birds of New Zealand,45</i>)

>  It answers somewhat that description of a hagdon, or shearwater, but is much larger, nearly the size of a goose. <i>(Jul 8, 1899,Poverty Bay Herald,2</i>)

### shed

 
<i>noun</i>. a wool shed

<i>verb</i>. [Rural] to separate or draft stock in the open paddock.

<i>verb</i>. [Rural] to place sheep in a woolshed prior to shearing or crutching, particularly if adverse weather is expected.

<i>noun</i>. a shearing contract

<i>noun</i>. a wharf storage shed.

<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a person in charge of a particular shearing [often the farm owner or manager, or a 'gang boss'].

>  <b>STUDHOLME</b> In the early days the manager acted as shed-boss. Later, when the agricultural work increased, a special shed-boss was engaged   <i>Ibid.</i> 127At Waimate there were about 50 men and boys employed for the shearing - 22 shearers, 1 sheep-oh, 4 fleece-pickers, 4 wool-rollers, 1 brander, 1 wool-classer, 1 classer's boy, 3 pressers, 1 waggoner, 1 cook, 1 cook's mate, generally known as the offsider or `slushy' 8 shepherds; and last, but not least the shed boss, ... [fn] In the early days the manager acted as shed boss. Later, when the agricultural work increased, a special shed boss was engaged. <i>(1940,Te Waimate,110,1954</i>)

>  <b>LANCASTER</b> A shed-boss must know all that breathes under the roof. <i>(1905,Sons o' Men,81</i>)

### shedding

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] the separating of a flock or mob into smaller sections or groups in a paddock.

>  Shedding system .... by which every ewe that lambs is immediately left behind, with others in like case, as the flock makes its daily trek on to the next paddock. <i>(Aug 7, 1957,Weekly News,34</i>)

>  <b>LILICO</b> [The dog] was no use in forcing, but at shedding and control of a small lot, he was perfect. <i>(1934,Sheep Dog Memoirs,5</i>)

>  It was what was called 'shedding' - ie separating different flocks that got mixed without taking them down to the pens. <i>(Aug 1884,Northern New Zealand Settler,241</i>)

>  Before penning, two sheep have to be separated - 'shedding' the sheep men call this operation - and confined to a circle apart from the others destined to be driven into the pen. <i>(Oct 27, 1938,NZ Farmer,9</i>)

>  <b>MILLS ET AL</b> Shedding, or separating the flock into respective lots might entail several different operations, depending on the topography of the country... <i>(1964,Practical Guide to Handling Dogs and Stock,97</i>)

>  <b>BEATTIE</b> There is a danger of all writers about the old days using modern terms which were not used in the period they are writing about. .... But some older writers make some surprising slips, and a really noticeable instance is in the inscription in the porch of the Memorial Church at Cave, South Canterbury, which reads: `This porch is erected to the glory of God in memory of the sheep-men, shepherds, bullock-drivers, shearers, and station-hands who pioneered the back-country of this province between the years 1855 and 1895' When I first read this inscription, the word `sheep-men' made me involuntarily flinch. Years later, when I had forgotten it, I suddenly met it again, and again I recoiled. So aghast was I that I spent weeks collecting every old term for `runholders' I could, and I found thirteen, viz., flock-owners, flock masters, pastoralists, run holders, run owners, sheep owners, sheep holders, sheep masters, squatters, station holders, station owners, stock holders and stock owners. The word `sheepmen' is a modern Americanism and using this anachronism mars a splendid memorial ..... Of all the thirteen terms found in old documents, the word `run holder' was the most used. <i>(1947,Early Runholding in Otago,11</i>)

Years later, when I had forgotten it, I suddenly met it again, and again I recoiled. So aghast was I that I spent weeks collecting every old term for `runholders' I could, and I found thirteen, viz., `flock owners,' `flock masters,' `pastoralists,' `run holders,' `run owners,' `sheep owners,' `sheep holders,' `sheep masters,' `squatters,' `station holders,' `station owners,' `stock holders,[sic] and `stock owners.' The word `sheepmen' is a modern Americanism, and using this anachronism mars a splendid memorial. ... Years later, when I had forgotten it, I suddenly met it again, and again I recoiled. So aghast was I that I spent weeks collecting every old term for `runholders' I could, and I found thirteen, viz., `flock owners,' `flock masters,' `pastoralists,' `run holders,' `run owners,' `sheep owners,' `sheep holders,' `sheep masters,' `squatters,' `station holders,' `station owners,' `stock holders,[sic] and `stock owners.' The word `sheepmen' is a modern Americanism, and using this anachronism mars a splendid memorial. ... [12] Of all the thirteen terms found in old documents, the word `runholder' was the most used, and it is the word that I think should be substituted. <i>(1947,Early Runholding in Otago,11</i>)

Years later, when I had forgotten it, I suddenly met it again, and again I recoiled. So aghast was I that I spent weeks collecting every old term for `runholders' I could, and I found thirteen, viz., `flock owners,' `flock masters,' `pastoralists,' `run holders,' `run owners,' `sheep owners,' `sheep holders,' `sheep masters,' `squatters,' `station holders,' `station owners,' `stock holders,[sic] and `stock owners.' The word `sheepmen' is a modern Americanism, and using this anachronism mars a splendid memorial. ... [12] Of all the thirteen terms found in old documents, the word `runholder' was the most used, and it is the word that I think should be substituted. <i>(1947,Early Runholding in Otago,11</i>)

>  <b>REES</b> The [shearing-] gang [included] ... some boys to act as `sheepo's' - that is to keep the pens in the shed filled up from the yards outside. <i>(1925,BLANK ENTRY,111</i>)

>  <b>STUDHOLME</b> The `sheep-oh' (penner-up) also held an important position. In addition to filling up the catching pens, he weighed the bales and recorded them, with their descriptions in the wool book. <i>Ibid.</i> 127 At Waimate there were about 50 men and boys employed for the shearing - 22 shearers, 1 sheep-oh, 4 fleece-pickers, 4 wool-rollers, 1 brander, 1 wool-classer, 1 classer's boy, 3 pressers, 1 waggoner, 1 cook, 1 cook's mate, generally known as the offsider or `slushy' 8 shepherds; and last, but not least the shed boss, ... [fn] In the early days the manager acted as shed boss. Later, when the agricultural work  increased, a special shed boss was engaged. <i>Ibid.</i> 130  The shearers were, of course, the autocrats of the shed, but the `sheep-oh' (penner-up) also held an important position. ### shellfish

 
<i>noun</i>.

[NOTES: An Australian lexicographer points out there is a difference between most dictionary definitions and what the public see as a shellfish; likewise in NZ the fishery regulations define for their convenience shellfish as including, from memory, crayfish, sponges and possibly even sea-grass. The sensible thing would be to redefine using as the basic definition the scientific one. The present OED definition is: Any animal living in water whose outer covering is a shell, whether testaceous, as an oyster, or crustaceous, as a crab. This wording is followed by Random House and Macquarie whereas the general public and scientists tend to think of a shellfish as a member of the class Mollusca, i.e. mostly animals with a hard calcareous shell or shells.]

### shepherd

 
<i>verb</i>.

>  <i>Shepherd</i>.- ... (2) To tail sheep by day and yard them at night. The<i> shepherding</i> system of sheep management was much employed in the early days of Australia, where the sheep would otherwise have been exposed to attack from blacks and dingoes. The <i>shagroons</i> (q.v.) carried it on to some extent on the Canterbury plains in the 'fifties, but soon gave it up for a system of <i>boundary keeping</i>, and afterwards fenced their runs. (C.) 3. To be a shepherd, e.g. `Bill is <i>shepherding</i> at __'s.' <i>(Dec 2, 1933,Press, The,15</i>) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]



 
<i>verb</i>.

<i>verb</i>. in various senses and applications within the general meaning `look after; watch over'

>  <b>WAYTE</b> Miss Amazon's instructions to her jockey were to `shepherd' the horse around the course. (ie. ride a waiting race .... The philologist would note that the word `shepherding' is of universal application in colonial parlance. If a stranger is lionised about a place, he is said to be `shepherded'. I once heard a man ask his neighbour to `shepherd' his grog while he left the room. It is of course natural that metaphors should be derived from the chief industries of the country.] <i>(1879,Prospecting for Gold,85</i>) [NOTES: 1879 Wayte Prospecting; or 18 Months in Australia and New Zealand 85]



 
<i>verb</i>.

<i>noun</i>.

>  <b>BEATTIE</b> The custom in the old days was to call the buildings on a run `the station,' and the land that went with it was `the run.' On a big property you could find several `stations,' and the principal one was called `the home station,' while the others were `out-stations.' This was the old Australian usage which was carried over to New Zealand at first, but gradually the signification was altered by loosely calling the whole run a station, and then the real station became a homestead and the out-stations became shepherds' huts. In this present book it will be noticed that generally the writer has preserved the olden custom of calling the main buildings the station and the land the run. The runs over in Australia being, as a rule, much larger than those in New Zealand, the `station' and `out-station' phraseology was preserved much longer than over here, where even in advertisements in the late 'fifties we see the English word `homestead' ousting the colonial word `station.' <i>Ibid.</i> 12 . provisions became `rations' ... when served out to the man at the `shepherds' huts' (or out-stations). <i>(1939,First White Boy Born in Otago,11</i>)

>  Sir, - I read `The Dominion's' second editorial of Jauary 25, `Our `She'll-Be-Right' Attitude,' with interest, but as a Grim Dig I feel that it is my duty to point out to the younger generation the origin and meaning of the expression `she's right' `She's right' or `She'll-Be- Right' originated in the Army and was only used when the person using the saying was satisfied that he had done his particular job to the best of his ability and took pride in it. If, on the other hand, he had done the job to the best of his ability but he was not satisfied with the job, he used the phrase `She's not too good' or `She's pretty poor' Never was the phrase `She's right' used in the sense that politicians and various other people not in the know use it to refer to a job badly done or done with a `couldn't-care-less' attitude. This was never necessary because in the Army we had other phrases to cover such contingencies when things did not go according to plan, such as NAFU and SAFU, the first being a non-adjusting fiasco, and the second being a self-adjusting fiasco. To say the least of it, I feel strongly that it is disrespectful to the originators of the saying `She's right' to use it in the present accepted sense, and I feel also that all Grim Digs should rise up in righteous wrath, but `don't do your scone boys.' Belmont. INFANTEER. <i>(Jan 30, 1963,Dominion,8</i>)

>  <i>she's right</i>: popular term to say that everything will be alright in the end; e.g., `She'll be right mate, don't worry about it.' <i>(1981,NZ Police National Headquarters</i>) [NOTES: (Goldie Brown Collection)]

>  <b>McGILL</b> right secure state philosophically important to traditional Kiwi person; I'll see you right reassurance that hospitality or a loan will be extended; she's right/she'll be right/she's jake/she's apples/she's sweet/too right all emphasising that all is secure and settled. NZA. <i>(1988,Dictionary of Kiwi Slang, A,92</i>)

>  'Get y'a beer?' 'Nah she's right thanks,' I say, giving my new full jug a nudge. <i>(2005,Huia 6: Contemp. Maori Fiction,29</i>)

>  The words he might have used, but didn't need to, are honoured shorthand on both sides of the Tasman: "She's right, mate."... So let's say to Bichel and to every Australian: "Good on ya, mate!" <i>(Mar 18, 2003,Dominion Post,B4</i>)

>  <b>LOCKWOOD</b> Yiddish became a main source of <i>Rotwelsch</i> [the cant language of thieves, etc.] In the course of time a number of originally cant words of Hebrew provenance passed into general use in German, though tending to remain at a more or less substandard level. Modern examples are colloquialisms like <i>acheln</i> eat, <i>Chuzpe</i> f. insolence, ... <i>mies</i> ugly, <i>Moos</i> n. money, <i>schicker </i>drunk, <i>schofel </i>trashy. These examples also occur in Standard Yiddish: <i>akhlen </i>(slang), <i>khutspe, ... mies, moes </i>(slang), <i>shiker, shofl. </i> <i>(1987,Informal History of the German Language, An,263</i>)

>  <b>ROSTEN</b> shikker Pronounced SHICK-er, to rhyme with `stick her'. Hebrew: <i>shikor</i>: `drunk1. A drunk. `He's a shikker.' 2. (Adjective) Drunk. `She got a wee bit<i> shikker</i>.' ... [349] <i>Shikkered</i>, to mean `drunk,' is commonly used in Australia [Wentworth and F 1960 p.466] How the word got all the way down to the Antipodes I do not know.] <i>(1971,Joys of Yiddish, The,348</i>)

### shicker

 
<i>noun</i>. a drunk

[NOTES: aka schicker, shikker]

>  Met a schicker last night. <i>(Sep 13, 1913,NZ Observer,16</i>)

>  In the world's wide ways of liquor / Leading downward to the Styx, / Be not like the casual shikker. / Turning home at stroke of six. <i>(Aug 19, 1926,NZ Truth,1</i>)

>  From time to time the Magistrate's Court hosted an absolutely shicker or two from the 6 o'clock swill of the day before. <i>(Oct 17, 1992,Evening Post,8</i>)



 
<i>adjective</i>. drunk

[NOTES: aka schicker, shikker, shickur, shickar et al]

>  He was coming up Manchester Street one night "a bit shikkar" when he dropped the watch, put his foot on it and broke it, and took it to a watchmaker for repairs, but that he had no money to pay with. <i>(Apr 8, 1897,Star, The,3</i>)

>  Both men were somewhat shikkur, so the sergeant asked them to move on. <i>(Apr 9, 1910,NZ Truth,7</i>)

>  No copper on the beat stood over a bloke because he was a bit shicker at 6.30. Being a bit shicker was quite different from being slightly P-word... If you were a bit shicker or even absolutely shicker at 6.30 it was because you had been having a good time with your mates over a few jugs. <i>(Oct 17, 1992,Evening Post,8</i>)

LOG-OF-WOOD) see also PLUNKET SHIELD, RANFURLY SHIELD [The Ranfurly Shield was presented by His Excellency the Earl of Ranfurly, Governor [?General] of New Zealand and patron of the NZ Rugby Football Union September 13 1902]

### shilling

 
<i>noun</i>. to express a degree of intellectual or mental handicap, or eccentricity, on the part of the addressee on a rough scale based on 20 shillings = 1 pound; and graded from say 1/6 IN THE POUND, TWO SHILLINGS IN THE POUND (of low intelligence, highly eccentric) to say NINETEEN SHILLINGS (slightly abnormal or missing): PAY variant from horseracing betting the metaphor resembles those implying that the person is NOT ALL THERE, is MISSING see also BOB, QUID, SHILLING; small entry only at POUND (check)

>  <b>McGILL</b> <i>shilling-a-month man</i> a remittance man, paid a shilling a month working his way on the ship out. The remittance man was often the black sheep of an English family, perhaps aristocratic, banished to a colony like New Zealand to live on a modest remittance from home. <i>(1888,Dictionary of Kiwi Slang, A,100</i>)

>  <b>HOWE</b> [MR. A. said] `I don't believe he is the full shilling' meaning, `I don't believe he has good sense' <i>(1913,Travel Letters,112</i>) [NOTES: AC 1942]

>  <b>DAVIN</b> He wasn't a bad bloke even if he was only fifteen bob in the pound. <i>(1947,For the Rest of Our Lives,118</i>)

>  <b>PARTRIDGE</b> <i>Shillings in the pound. eighteen</i> or, say, <i>twelve and six</i>, to indicate slight mental dullness or mild insanity; `He's only twelve and six in the pound': New Zealand: since ca. 1925. Niall Alexander, Oct. 22, 1939. <i>(1949,Dictionary of Slang Addenda,1166</i>)

>  <b>SLATTER</b> Every small town has its characters: ... Possum who only came out at night, Joey who was eighteen shillings, ... the local pervert, the local anarchist. <i>(1968,Pagan Game, The,153</i>)

>  <b>HUNT</b> He used to tell the story of one old bloke who wasn't quite twenty bob in the pound, a sort of village idiot. <i>(1981,Speaking a Silence,95</i>)

>  <b>McGILL</b> <i>shillings in the pound</i> dull or somewhat insane; a specified figure is given, eg `He's only 12 shillings/bob in the pound.' C.1925. <i>(1988,Dictionary of Kiwi Slang, A,100</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. a semi-circular notch in an axe-blade

### shingle

 
<i>noun</i>. coarse gravel

>  Waimate Road Board. Committee met (Chairman and Mr Stewart) on Wednesday, 20th April, when following tenders were opened and dealt with:- .. 190 Eltham Road, R. Warner, broken stone, 5s 6d (accepted); shingle, 3s 9d; Brough and Whittington, stone, 6s 3d; shingle, 3s 3d; Dillon and Humphries, 6s 9d; shingle, 5s; B. Sheerin, shingle, 4s 9d. <i>(Apr 21, 1898,Hawera & Normanby Star,2</i>)

>  The height of the Tararua was computed to be three thousand feet above the level of the sea. It was covered with shingle and a heavy growth of black birch. <i>(Aug 22, 1840,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,2</i>)

>  Tenders are invited by the Government architect for the supply of shingle and sand, and delivery of the same, at Mount View, Wellington. <i>(Jun 4, 1909,Evening Post,7</i>) [NOTES: Advert]

>  <b>Owen Marshall</b>  <i>(2009,Living As A Moon,28</i>) [NOTES: Faster and faster, but when we got to scree slope, where it's better to cross on the trot when the shingle and rocks start to move, I left him lagging behind.]

>  <b>TURNER</b> <i>Bush-line</i> or sometimes [161] <i>forest-line</i> (for American <i>timber-line</i>, English<i> tree-line </i>and Australian <i>tree-line</i> or <i>forest-line), bush-clad, bush burns</i> (areas where the bush has recently been burnt off) are tramping as well as general terms, as is the use of <i>shingle</i> for angular as well as rounded stones in <i>shingle slide</i>, or (earlier) <i>shingle slip</i>, also recently called scree as in Scotland and northern England. eg. 1890-1910 Ac. Loose, rather sharp, shale or similar rock. Much more widely used in NZ than C.O.D. `small rounded pebbles on sea-shore', esp. in loose combinations, or attributively eg shingle tops, basins, facings etc (Ac) <i>(1966,English Language in Aust. & NZ, The,160</i>)

>  <b>HAAST</b> In examining these angular fragments (usually called shingle in New Zealand, whence the expression `shingle slips' for these huge taluses of debris covering the mountain sides), we find that they have a polyhedrical shape, their planes being sharply defined, and cutting, as seen in the conglomerates, clean through even the hardest pebbles of which the latter are composed. <i>(1879,Geology of the Provinces of Canterbury & Westland,174</i>)

>  Light loam, shingle and gravel subsoil. <i>(Mar 1849,Torlesse Papers,64,1958</i>)

>  <b>GOLDIE</b> ... Titaroi, whose singularly looking shingle upon its top brings it the appellation of `Whitehead' <i>(1863,Diary</i>) [NOTES: 1863 Goldie's Diary in 1947 Beattie The Pioneers Explore Otago 141]

>  <i>Shingle</i>.- Loose, rather sharp shale or similar rock. Hence <i>S.tops, shingle basins, sy. facings,</i> etc. <i>(Dec 2, 1933,Press, The,15</i>) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]

>  <b>THOMSON</b> I went towards the head of the valley, carefully picking my way through a large rock slide, when up above me I heard the sound of moving shingle. <i>(1982,Deer Hunter: The Experiences of a NZ Stalker,74</i>)

>   <i>(1959,Tararua,13/46</i>)

<i>noun</i>. [Rural] [high country pastoral land] sharp angular shale shattered from basic rock.

<i>noun</i>. a piece of split (now also sawn) wood, usually rectangular used for roofing is general English (OED from 1200) but OED quotations (esp. in combinations) seem to have a provincial, and later a `colonial' flavour, although the sense does not occur in EDD. Certainly in early NZ, shingles were perhaps the commonest roofing material. British observers in the 19th century often feel obliged to explain the term. e.g.

>  <b>FORSTER</b> The latter [sc. argillaceous slate] is commonly found in great quantity, and broken pieces, on the sea beaches, and is what our seamen call shingle, by which name it is distinguished in the account of captain Cook's former voyage. <i>(1777,Voyage Round the World,1/204</i>)

>  <b>WILLIAMS</b> Mr Fairburn tried the <i>Tanakaha</i> to split for shingles ... <i>(Jul 23, 1828,Early Journals of Henry Williams, The,139,1961</i>)

>  <b>WILLIAMS</b> ?collective Mr. Davis ... and a party of natives went up the river in quest of timber for the purpose of making shingle. <i>(Sep 17, 1828,Early Journals of Henry Williams, The,144,1961</i>)

>  ... houses built mostly of wood ... but generally painted white outside, and roofed with `shingles' (flat squares of wood), which from exposure to the weather looks like slate. <i>(Dec 17, 1848,Letters from Otago,23,1978</i>)

>  <b>WAKEFIELD</b> ... shingles, N.Z. [per] 1000, 6s. to 8s. ... whalebone [per] ton, 135l. to 140l. - finners, 40l. <i>(1848,Handbook for New Zealand, The,180</i>)

>  Some [houses] are merely covered with grass, others built with clay, others weather boarded, ... and for slates we have shingles, or a sort of lath one foot long, 4 inches broad, 1/4-inch thick; ... <i>(Apr 16, 1849,Letters from Otago,31,1978</i>)

>  EMIGRATION BARRACKS will be commenced both here and at Christchurch as soon as ... timber, 300,000 shingles and 16 carpenters, which have been ordered from Hobart Town, arrive. <i>(Aug 23, 1849,Torlesse Papers,98/5,1958</i>)

>  A material feature in these shingles is their economy: ... They are as durable as ordinary English slates, and cover the same surface at half the expense. <i>(May 31, 1851,Lyttelton Times,7</i>)

>  <b>HIGGINS</b> The roof is covered with shingles, which is wood made into pieces about 12 inches long and 6 inches wide and of course thin. These are nailed one over the other like tiles. <i>(Dec 27, 1858,Letters</i>) [NOTES: (Griffiths Collection)]

>  The bed [of the Racia] is two miles across, the water a mile but split up into many branches. The water is melted snow; ... and roars along ... over large boulders, quicksands, shingle and stumps of trees. <i>(Mar 16, 1862,Chudleigh Diary,28,1950</i>)

>  I got here [Mount Brown Station] ... fortunately there were carts going up to the run with shingles (wooden tiles) so I got my swag up free and trudged myself. <i>(Nov 10, 1862,Journal and Letters (Walker)</i>) [NOTES: (Mt Brown, Canterbury)]

>  <b>AYLMER</b> It was a cottage roofed with `cob' or `shingle' as it is often called; namely little pieces of wood in the shape of slates. <i>(1862,Distant Homes,60</i>)

>  <b>COLLINSON</b> Houses are generally built throughout the colony of a frame-work of timber, weather-boarded outside, and roofed with shingles <i>(1853,Military Operations in NZ,29</i>)

>  <b>BARKER</b> [He] found the roof, tore off some shingles, and returned with a few aged hens ... <i>(1867,Station Life in NZ,163,1870</i>)

>  <i>Blenheim Timber Yard</i>. ... Straining and Fencing Posts and Rails ... Shingles and Piles. <i>(Jan 4, 1868,Marlborough Express,8</i>)

>  <b>KENNAWAY</b> ... not having been initiated into the art of putting on shingles for a roof, ... we secured a professional shingler from the port town. <i>(1874,Crusts: a settler's fare due south,22</i>)

>  <b>A LADY</b> Habitations with wooden walls and `wooden tiles', locally called shingles. <i>(1882,Facts Relating to NZ,8</i>)

>  <b>BARLOW</b> Instead of slates or tiles, thin strips of wood, called shingles, split off small blocks of Kauri, are most commonly used for the roofing ... <i>(1888,Kaipara and Waitemata Echo,177</i>)

>  <b>REEVES</b> <i>Shingles</i> [FN], pieces of split wood 10' x 3 [and a half]' x [a quarter]' used for roofing. <i>(1892,Homeward Bound,63</i>)

>  <b>SALMOND</b> <i>Shingle</i>. a machine sawn <i>shake. </i> <i>(1986,Glossary of Building Terminology,233</i>)

>  <b>SCOTT</b> <i>Shingles</i> Thin, oblong, tapered pieces of wood produced by sawing and used in covering roofs and outer walls. Western red ceder shingles are commonly imported into New Zealand. <i>(1987,Imported Timbers,73</i>)

### shingle short, a

 
<i>phrase</i>. .

See: take a shingle off

[NOTES: aka a shingle off, a shingle loose.  1953 16 M A33 Thames DHS 2 SHINGLE SHORT (with variations) `a screw loose' perhaps deriving from <i>have a tile loose</i>, with shingle a metaphor for head or hair (cf thatch); or from be a bit short, missing on top; to be not all there (on top)]

>  A man would have been thought a shingle short if he had said 15 or 20 years ago that the present reapers and binders would be invented ... <i>(Jun 13, 1889,Otago Witness,34</i>)

>  The same member of the Board, later on, speaking of another tenant, said that after a conversation of half an hour's duration with the tenant the conviction came to him that "the tenant should have been a shingle-splitter instead of a selector - for he was a shingle short!" <i>(Dec 2, 1901,Wanganui Herald,2</i>)

>  Fool, idiot, lunatic, daft, "shingle short,' are easily said. <i>(Jul 3, 1876,North Otago Times,2</i>)

>  Is the man sane who wrote it, or has he a shingle off, or does he suffer from some severe hallucination of the brain? <i>(May 17, 1876,Grey River Argus,2</i>)

>  John Smith Harris, known to the foolish as the "Whiffler," hereby gives public notice that, if anyone who is worth powder and shot states in the presence of witnesses - and he (J.S.H.) has plenty on the look out - that Mr Harris has a "screw lose [sic]," "a tile short," "a shingle off the roof," "a bee in his bonnet," or that "he is not in his right mind," by the powers he'll go for them, straight from the shoulder. <i>(Jan 7, 1885,Manawatu Standard,2</i>)

>  .. in short it was his firm opinion that Maitai himself could not be held responsible for his actions; and he should very soon begin to think that those who advanced him money were, in vulgar parlance 'a shingle short.' <i>(Oct 15, 1861,Colonist, The,2</i>)

>  No, Melisande, Sancho Panza is not the patron saint of the German talk divisions.   He rode an ass and his master, Don Quixote, a sorry steed, but although the Don was a shingle short and tilted at windmills, he was a kind-hearted, chivalrous gentleman, which is more than can be said of the Nazi panzer commanders. <i>(Nov 29, 1941,Evening Post,8</i>)

>  As a matter of fact half the people in the world have a shingle loose somewhere, and if an evil gust happens to strike them just there the whole brain may be unroofed. <i>(Apr 5, 1892,Bruce Herald,2</i>)

>  Screws loose in the head are rivetted. Shingles off are fixed. <i>(1865,Punch in Canterbury,73</i>)

>  We think there are more shingles loose than he speaks of <i>(1865,Punch in Canterbury,7/24</i>)

>  <b>THATCHER</b> (Christchurch Signboards) And here you have a <i>Thatcher/</i> If you're a shingle short! <i>(1862,Canterbury Songster,2</i>)

>  <b>LYTTELTON</b> Mr. Acland used an odd colonial phrase for a half-witted person: `shingle-short'. Wooden shingles being used, like the wooden church-spires in Kent and Sussex, for house-roofs, it means, weak in the head. <i>(1868,Two Lectures,34</i>)

>  <b>GRACE</b> I smiled, and ranked him [an eccentric major] a shingle short. <i>(1899,Sketch of the NZ War,22</i>)

>  <b>18</b> <i>shingle short, to be a v.</i>not completely balanced mentally. <i>(1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins)</i>)

>  <b>McGILL</b> <i>shingle, short</i>, a mentally deficient. NZA. <i>(1988,Dictionary of Kiwi Slang, A,101</i>)

>  <b>LYTTELTON</b> Mr. Acland used an odd colonial phrase for a half-witted person: `shingle-short' Wooden shingles being used, like wooden church-spires in Kent and Sussex, for house-roofs, it means, weak in the head. <i>(1868,Two Lectures,34</i>)

>  <b>COTTLE</b> He was a `shingle short' without doubt <i>(1891,Frank Melton's Luck,6</i>)

>  <b>BAUGHAN</b> <i>Shingle-short</i>: Australasian for `a tile loose.' <i>Anglice</i>: Wanting in intellect. Aj. <i>(1908,Shingle-Short,11</i>)

### shingle slip

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a steep slide of running scree or loose stones [usually on high mountain or hill country. ]

>  Turning a little along the ridge to the left, we descended a steep shingle slip of some 300 or 400 feet, and following down a gully with loose stones, alpine plants, and finally black birch, found ourselves, by about four, p.m., on the S.E side of the range, and to our joy, once more upon the banks of the East Wairau, which here pierces right through the mountains, and leads directly to our camp of the morning. <i>(Jun 2, 1855,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,2</i>)

>  The runs on [t]he east side of Lake Tekapo are [s]till practically wholly white, the only contrasts being shingle slips, new slips and wind-swept rocks. <i>(Aug 26, 1895,North Otago Times,1</i>)

>  <b>BARKER</b> .. a deep drift of snow still lingered, filling up a furrow made in former years by a shingle-slip. <i>(1873,Station Amusements in NZ,82</i>)

>  .. the sub-alpine shingle-slips have increased in size. <i>(Jan 20, 1919,NZ Journal of Agriculture,6</i>)

>  <b>MCCASKILL</b> Do not burn on greywacke mountains in the vicinity of shingle-slips or where the soil is hallow and slips are already made. <i>(1920,Hold This Land,151,(1973)</i>) [NOTES: Report App. House Reps]

>  <b>MCCASKILL</b> On open plains and sunny hill faces this [soil diminishing] has led to accelerated wind and frost erosion and on higher mountain slopes to increased down-hill creep of shingle slips and mantles of waste. [shingle-slip] <i>(1973,Hold This Land,4</i>)

>  With the possible exception of certain littoral and alpine shingle slip plants, Otari presents a wealth of conditions suitable for our native plants from rainforest, alpine, swamp, and sub-tropical areas. <i>(Aug 17, 1939,Evening Post,27</i>)

>  <b>TURNER</b> <i>Bush-line</i> or sometimes [161] <i>forest-line</i> (for American <i>timber-line,</i> English <i>tree-line</i> and Australian <i>tree-line</i> or <i>forest-line), bush-clad, bush burns</i> (areas where the bush has recently been burnt off) are tramping as well as general terms, as is the use of <i>shingle </i>for angular as well as rounded stones in <i>shingle slide</i>, or (earlier) <i>shingle slip</i>, also recently called scree as in Scotland and northern England. <i>(1966,English Language in Aust. & NZ, The,160</i>)

>  <b>COCKAYNE</b> Shingle-slip, in its unstable typical form, is confined to those mountains of South Island with a tussock-grassland climate and is most strongly in evidence in the North-eastern and Eastern districts. <i>(1928,Vegetation of New Zealand, The,289</i>)

>  <b>HOOKER</b> Shingle slips, Wairau Gorge, alt. 4500 ft. [Travers.] <i>(1864,Handbook NZ Flora,11</i>)

>  <b>HAAST</b> The shingle-slips ... are also not without an interesting vegetation .<i>Ibid.</i> ..  174 In examining these angular fragments (usually called shingle in New Zealand, whence the expression `shingle slips' for these huge taluses of debris covering the mountain sides), we find that they have a polyhedrical shape, their planes being sharply defined, and cutting, as seen in the conglomerates, clean through even the hardest pebbles of which the latter are composed. <i>(1879,Geology of the Provinces of Canterbury & Westland,36</i>)

>  At times we were scrambling through the thick bush or over steep shingle slips. <i>(1885,TrNZI,17/352</i>) [NOTES: (Park)]

>  One of the most characteristic features of our Canterbury Alps is afforded by the numerous `shingle-slips' formed by the weathering of the rocks, and often covering almost entire hill-sides. <i>(1900,Canterbury Old & New,190</i>)

>  <b>COCKAYNE</b> As the traveller wearily ascends these `shingle-slips', as they are called, the stones constantly slip beneath his tread, ... <i>(1910,NZ Plants,97</i>)

>  The old and mature shingle-slips are far larger than those now existing. <i>(1908,TrNZI,40/38</i>) [NOTES: (Speight)]

>  Votes of thanks were passed to Mr David Stevenson, Caversham, for promissory note by John Jones for GBP1, payable at Dunedin or Waikouaiti three days after date - those notes (sometimes called shin plasters) were in the form of a bank note, and were in circulation until January 2, 1857 ... <i>(Aug 5, 1908,Otago Witness,14</i>)

>  Depend upon it, fellow colonists, if they could not keep their mercurial fingers off the sacred fund of the widows and orphans, they will have small respect for those provisions of the Colonial Ordinance which professedly provide a security for the payment of the shin plasters. <i>(Jun 29, 1850,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,69</i>)

>  He hurled denunciations at the head of Sir John in particular, and the Stock Exchange in general, and in heroic language declared that New Zealand was a self-reliant, non-borrowing colony, and that Sir John and the Stock Exchange could depart for Sheol forthwith, and that he and Seddon and M'Kenzie could run the show by the aid of Consols, Postal notes, and shin plasters of a variety of patterns till further orders, and be d--d to him. <i>(Apr 19, 1895,Evening Post,4</i>)

>  A feature of the exhibit is a number of debentures or "shin plasters" as they were irreverently termed, which were put  into circulation during the term of the governorship of Captain Fitzroy...  The Government debentures  were for 5s, but the private ones were for sums ranging down as low as 3d. <i>(Feb 20, 1890,Otago Daily Times,17</i>)

>  But these war advances we got from J.B. were, perhaps, part of the shin plaster J.B. borrowed from Uncle Sam, and Downie Stewart may have learned from U.S.'s pawnbrokers exactly how England funded her huge war debt with them. <i>(Jun 27, 1925,NZ Truth,5</i>)

>  And Sir Samuel/Hoare - he goes / With shin plaster / On his nose ... <i>(Dec 18, 1935,Evening Post,8</i>)

>  <b>JOSEPH MASTERS</b> Many tradesmen [in the early 1840s] had to make their own money on strips of paper called by the settlers `shin plaisters'. Governor Grey [sic] established a bank issue and issued one pound promisery [sic] notes, to get change for one of these, you would get a hat full of shin plaisters. <i>(1871,Autobiography,26</i>)

>  <b>MACDONALD</b> I do not know exactly how wholesale mercantile business was carried on, but the retail business in the town [?Wellington] was carried on [c1840s] mostly by means of little bits of printed paper, issued by shopkeepers, for from one penny to two or three shillings. This currency went by the general name of `shin plaster'. <i>Ibid.</i> 117 When eggs fell from six silver shillings per dozen to one shilling of `shin plasters', the Hutt, Porirua Road and Karori settlers looked anxious. <i>(1910,Reminiscences,109</i>) [NOTES: c1840s in c1910 Macdonald Reminiscences (TS:VUW) 109]

>  <b>SUTHERLAND</b> <i>Shinplasters</i>.- The fact that private traders found it necessary themselves, to issue paper notes in denominations below five shillings suggests that at the outset ... the Fitzroy notes were not issued for values below five shillings. The private paper notes were issued for small change, redeemable mostly in `Five Shillings, in Government debentures.' Both the debentures and the private notes were issued on poor paper, and soon became known as `Government Rags' and `Shinplasters' respectively. The term `Shinplaster' for paper money appears to have come to New Zealand from America, via New South Wales. *[fn] In the latter Colony the issue of paper money of a denomination lower than twenty shillings was prohibited in 1826 to promote the circulation of sterling instead of a colonial currency, and the prohibition was welcomed by the people as `preventing the Colony being inundated with beggarly rags' and dollar and half-dollar notes `used often as a paltry contrivance to evade payment of debt,' <i>vide "The Australian," </i>19 July 1826. [fn] Various reasons have been given for the origin of this curious term for paper money issued in the forties. The most likely explanation comes from America (p. 650 <i>The Numismatist,</i> 1938), where it is stated that in the good old days post-boys and out-riders, wearing high boots, were required, at times, to pay toll-fees at toll-gates, and in order to facilitate progress they placed paper money or coins in bags in their boot-tops, against their shins - hence the term `shin-plaster.' <i>(1941,Numismatic History of NZ,158</i>)

>  <b>HARGREAVES</b> The [Governor Fitzroy's (1844)] Debentures, popularly known as `government rags', were given various nicknames such as<i> assignats,</i> `shinplasters', and `flash notes'. All these terms had reference to worthless paper money, some of which had been issued in the past. <i>Assignats</i> was the name given to large amounts of paper money issued in France during the French Revolution, but which depreciated to such as extent to be almost worthless. `Shinplasters' - sometimes written `skinplasters' - had its origin in North America, and again referred to depreciated paper money, while `flash notes' was a popular term in use for any counterfeit money or worthless forged paper money. <i>(1972,From Beads to Banknotes,40</i>)

### shloop

 
<i>noun</i>. slurpy movement and sound

>  (Speaking of Sir James Hector)  He must have had a very strong stomach for he mentioned once how they had cooked wekas . . . . I had found them quite palatable if you could get rid of the rich strong grease.  He said they put a stone inside the body which caused the melted grease to accumulate there.  'Then', I said, 'you could throw it away'.  'Oh; no,  oh, no' and cupping his hands to his mouth he showed how you could hold the bird's body upside down and then: shloop! . . . .' <i>(Apr 1966,Geological Society of NZ Newsletter,20/3</i>)

>  <b>Stephen Judd</b> With a soft shloop the entire viscera, lungs, guts, and all would bulge, resist and then give way, falling in a shiny heap on to the offal table below. <i>(Oct 2005,Internet - see Notes,3</i>) [NOTES: www.vital.org.nz/meat.html  No dates on page.]

### shoe

 
<i>noun</i>. snigging pan

>  When logs are to be hauled up to logging bank, a stout steel dog is driven into the end of the log, which lies on a broad steel shoe, and as the engine winds its load forward this shoe rides over every obstacle in the track until the log or logs (mostly two or three at a time) are brought out of the bush on to tram line to be conveyed to the sawmill. <i>(Jul 3, 1901,Otago Witness,60</i>)

>  He heaved up the shoe - which is a much over-grown road-scoop tilted at the nose. <i>(1905,Sons o' Men,165</i>)

>   <i>(1952,NZ Forest Glossary</i>)

>  <b>SANSOM</b> Behind one heap of fireplace stones is a whale's skull, once used as a `shoe' to bring out logs. <i>(1982,In the Grip of an Island,32</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a cover placed on a tractor wheel.

>  <b>ARTHUR</b> We had to put some 'shoes' on the tractor as the tracks were tearing up the grass paddocks too much. <i>(1984,Waiouru: Land of the Tussock 1935-40,20</i>)

### shoemaker

 
<i>noun</i>. species of petrel

>  <b>JENKIN</b> The identity of this bird [hakuwai] is still in doubt. Most of the petrels have been suggested at some stage, including the bird the whalers called the Shoemaker because of the tapping noise it made, but the New Zealand Wildlife Service now believe the <i>hakuwai</i> to be the Stewart Island snipe, thought to be extinct. <i>(1970,NZ Mysteries,157</i>)

>  <i>White-chinned Petrel Procellaria aequinoctialis</i> LINNAEUS, 1758. ... OTHER NAMES:<i> Shoemaker, Cape hen</i>. .... DISTRIBUTION <i>Breeds at the Auckland Islands ... the Falkland Islands ... </i> <i>(1985,Reader's Digest Book of NZ Birds,92</i>)
